China policy, opposition unity will be Cheng's main challenges: KMT sources
Taipei, Oct. 18 (CNA) Former Legislator Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文), who was elected chairperson of the opposition Kuomintang (KMT) on Saturday, will face two main challenges in her new role -- the main one being the party's stance on China affairs, according to sources within the KMT.
Apart from the China issue, the other major challenge for the new KMT leader will be whether she can forge cooperation with the smaller opposition Taiwan People's Party (TPP) to lead the KMT back into power, a KMT insider told CNA on condition of anonymity.
Cheng beat five other candidates, including another front runner -- two-time Taipei Mayor Hau Lung-bin (郝龍斌) -- to win the race and become the second woman to be elected as party chairperson, following Hung Hsiu-chu (洪秀柱), who served from 2016 to 2017.
With Cheng as leader of the main opposition party, other members who plan to run in the future against candidates from the ruling pro-independence Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) are likely to encounter pressure, the KMT source said, noting that Cheng has been known to call on people in Taiwan to identify as "Chinese."
During the chairperson election campaign, Cheng was embroiled in controversy over her stance on China affairs and her alleged affiliation with Beijing.
At one point, KMT heavyweight and TV personality Jaw Shau-kong (趙少康) accused China of interfering in the election and implied that Beijing favored Cheng.
According to the KMT source, Cheng will need to tackle such internal controversies, devise a clear cross-strait policy, and work to unite the different factions within the party.
In addition, the source said, the party's future leadership direction will differ somewhat from the past, and it may take some time for party members to adapt, given that she was a DPP member until 2002, after which she joined the KMT in 2005.
Meanwhile, a KMT city councilor, who asked not to be named, said Cheng needs to consider how to work with the TPP to defeat the "green camp," referring to the DPP.
For example, the councilor said, there is the imminent question of whether the KMT would decide not to compete against the TPP for some seats in the 2026 local government elections, to improve the opposition parties' chances of winning the majority of seats.
More importantly, cooperation between the blue and the white camps -- the KMT and the TPP -- will be critical in the presidential election in 2028 if they are to oust the DPP, the councilor said.
In 2024, the DPP won the presidential election, with Lai Ching-te (賴清德) gaining 40.05 percent of the votes, after the KMT and TPP failed to form a joint ticket. The KMT's Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜) and the TPP's Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) secured 33.49 percent and 26.46 percent of votes, respectively, totaling 59.95 percent.
According to another source within the KMT, the century-old party needs a facelift, and Cheng is the right person to do that. At age 55, she is younger than most of the KMT heavyweights and is seen as a good successor to the previous party leaders, the source said.
The KMT has been in opposition for the past nine years, having lost the last three presidential elections to the DPP, the source noted. There are high hopes within the KMT that Cheng, who presents as a fighter, will help the KMT win the next presidential election, according to the source.
Cheng will start her four-year term as leader of the KMT on Nov. 1, succeeding incumbent chairman Eric Chu (朱立倫).

China-Taiwan Weekly Update, October 20, 2025
Institute for the Study of War
October 20, 2025
Data Cutoff: October 18, 2025
The China–Taiwan Weekly Update is a joint product from the Institute for the Study of War and the American Enterprise Institute. The update supports the ISW–AEI Coalition Defense of Taiwan project, which assesses Chinese campaigns against Taiwan, examines alternative strategies for the United States and its allies to deter the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) aggression, and—if necessary—defeat the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). The update focuses on the Chinese Communist Party’s paths to controlling Taiwan and cross–Taiwan Strait developments.
Toplines
PRC manufacturers have dramatically increased fiber optic drone component exports to Russia, possibly indicating a heightened PRC commitment to Russian battlefield success in Ukraine. The Washington Post released a report on October 13 citing official PRC trade data that showed that the PRC exported 119,000 miles of fiber optic cable to Russia in May 2025, 130,000 miles in June 2025, and 328,000 miles in August 2025.[1] PRC fiber optic exports to Russia peaked at 87,000 miles in September 2024 before this summer and had dwindled to 7,000 miles in March 2025.[2] The Washington Post reported that PRC lithium-ion battery exports to Russia also increased substantially in June 2025.[3] Both components are crucial to producing fiber optic drones, which are resistant to electronic jamming.[4] The Russian military continues to saturate the frontline in Ukraine with fiber optic drones that can perform tactical strikes and battlefield interdiction at ranges up to 12 kilometers.[5] ISW reported that Russia is attempting to increase the scale of its fiber optic drone production to enhance battlefield effectiveness and counter large Ukrainian bomber drones.[6] The substantial increase in PRC fiber optic drone components to Russia this summer may reflect a concentrated PRC effort to support this Russian procurement strategy.
Ukrainian telegram channel “Powerful Informant” claimed on October 7 that PRC-produced radars were found deployed with Russian counter-drone units near Russia’s Belgorod Oblast on the border of Kharkiv Oblast.[7] The alleged PRC radars are the Zhejiang Fanshuang Technology Co. FSTH-LD02 and FSTH-LD03 that are designed for all-weather small target detection at ranges between 5 and 10 km.[8] Ukrainian source Defense Express claimed these radars were the “eyes” of Russian FPV counter-drone units.[9]
ISW assessed that the PRC has a vested strategic interest in supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine to keep US attention divided between Europe and the Indo-Pacific.[10] The PRC has provided dual-use exports to Russia’s defense industrial base, such as semiconductors and electronic diodes, and possibly satellite reconnaissance.[11] Sixty percent of foreign components found in Russian military equipment originated in the PRC, according to Ukrainian officials.[12]
A marked increase in drone-related support for Russia’s war in Ukraine may indicate that the PRC has determined that it must provide more tangible support to Russia’s military if it is to achieve its objectives. The PRC may seek to enable Russia’s ability to continue prosecuting the war in Ukraine amid increased US pressure to conclude a ceasefire to the conflict. Increased PRC drone exports also follow heightened US and European efforts to provide greater material support to Ukraine.[13] The Ukrainian battlefield may act as a testing ground for PRC drone components to integrate lessons from an active conflict for future drone production. Russia and the PRC have previously collaborated on Kevlar-reinforced fiber optic cables to improve drone operations in difficult terrain.[14]
The PRC expanded its export controls over rare earths ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, highlighting how the CCP uses its market dominance for economic coercion and can disrupt the international flow of critical materials that are essential to many advanced technologies. The PRC Commerce Ministry announced on October 9 export controls on holmium, europium, ytterbium, thulium, and erbium as well as equipment to refine and process such materials.[15] This is the first time that the PRC has included export controls over technologies related to critical mineral processing.[16] The export controls apply to items produced outside the PRC using 0.1 percent or more PRC-sourced rare earth materials by value, thereby requiring foreign firms using rare earth materials to also apply for export licenses.[17] The PRC Commerce Ministry also announced export controls on certain lithium-ion batteries, graphite anodes, and synthetic diamonds the same day. [18] The PRC previously placed export controls on seven lanthanides—a series of rare earth metals—in April 2025. Twelve of 17 rare earths are now under PRC export controls.[19]
The CCP is using the export controls over rare earths to gain leverage in its trade negotiations with the United States and coerce the United States into making concessions. The United States—and many other countries—rely heavily on the PRC for rare earths, which are in turn essential to many advanced technologies and modern economies. Seventy percent of US rare-earth imports from 2020 to 2023 were from the PRC.[20] The United States will continue to be vulnerable to this kind of economic coercion so long as it remains reliant on the PRC for rare earths.
CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are scheduled to meet in-person at the upcoming APEC summit. Trump had responded to the critical mineral export controls by stating “there seems to be no reason” to meet with Xi on October 10, but he has since confirmed on October 17 that the APEC meeting will still happen.[21] Trump initially responded to the latest PRC export controls by threatening to impose 100-percent tariffs targeting the PRC but has since called that figure unsustainable, and revised the tariff threat to “a very high number.”[22]
South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young confirmed that the Lee Jae Myung administration will pursue a two-state framework for inter-Korean relations on October 14.[29] South Korea has continued to pursue rapprochement with North Korea and offer conciliatory gestures, though North Korean leads have continued to express disinterest in dialogue. Unification Minister Chung emphasized the importance of peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula, as a step towards unification.[30] Unification Minister Chung added that adopting a two-state solution would create an opportunity for peace based on President Lee Jae Myung’s END (exchange, normalization, denuclearization) Initiative.[31] The Office of the South Korean President replied that this issue was for the responsibility of the Unification Ministry, implicitly suggesting that the framework would become part of the Lee administration’s North Korea policy.[32] The Unification Ministry separately announced plans to reorganize and restore offices dedicated to inter-Korean exchange and removing the office focused on addressing North Korean human rights issues.[33]
Unification Minister Chung’s “peaceful two-state framework” aims for mutual recognition of statehood and peaceful coexistence between South Korea and North Korea. Chung further said on September 29 that South Korea needs to “acknowledge the reality” of the North Korean nuclear weapons program.[34] This shift in North Korea policy suggests that the Lee administration may be gradually moving away from the long-standing South Korean unification policy while instead focusing heavily on denuclearization.
North Korea has rejected Lee administration attempts for dialogue and has considered South Korea an “enemy state” in its constitution since 2024.[35] North Korea also established the “hostile two-state framework” on December 31, abandoning its previously stated unification goals.[36] North Korea may leverage the Lee administration’s conciliatory approach to extract further concessions. Continued unilateral concessions and policy changes could undermine South Korean security. Members of the Lee administration have suggested reducing training and altering force structure near the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which could leave South Korea vulnerable to North Korean provocation.
Former Kuomintang (KMT) legislator Cheng Li-wun won the KMT chairperson election on October 18, defeating establishment favorite Hau Lung-bin. Cheng is a vocal advocate for a shared “Chinese” identity for Taiwanese people. KMT members voted on October 18 on a new party chair to replace current Chairman Eric Chu, who did not seek reelection. Cheng Li-wun won decisively with 50.15 percent of the vote.[37] She will be sworn in at the KMT party caucus in November.[38] Cheng’s closest rivals, former Taipei mayor Hau Lung-bin and current KMT legislator Lo Chih-chiang, respectively received 35.85 and 10.4 percent of the vote.[39] September polling mostly showed Hau in the lead, but Cheng rapidly overtook him in the polls in the last several weeks.[40] Polling conducted throughout October showed that Cheng’s support had grown to around twice the support for Hau.[41]
Cheng leaned more heavily into “Chinese identity” than other candidates. She said on October 8 that all Taiwanese citizens are Chinese, according to the constitution, and that she would make every Taiwanese “proud to call themselves Chinese.”[42] Hau clarified in response that it was important to distinguish between Chinese cultural and political identity. Cheng aligns with her party and other candidates in support of the 1992 Consensus, an alleged KMT-CCP verbal agreement that Taiwan is part of “One China” but with differing interpretations of which government rightfully represents “China.” Cheng also said that Taiwan’s defense spending should not exceed three percent of GDP, the lowest limit proposed by any of the top candidates.[43]
Cheng Li-wun’s popularity appeared to be buoyed by a popular perception that she represents “generational turnover” for the KMT and could revitalize the party after three consecutive presidential election defeats.[44] Hau was most likely the KMT establishment favorite, prominently backed by KMT firebrand and former vice presidential candidate Jaw Shaw-kong, legislative caucus whip Fu Kun-chi, and many local faction leaders.[45] Hau is in his 70s, nearly 20 years older than Cheng. Former President Ma Ying-jeou endorsed Lo, his former aide, and offered encouragement to Hau.[46]
KMT chairman candidates and other KMT figures alleged possible CCP interference in the chairperson election. Candidate Hau Lung-bin claimed on October 11 that his campaign was being attacked by fake news, fake polls, and cyber operations originating from “abroad” and possibly organized by fellow party members.[53] His chief backer, Jaw Shaw-kong, said more explicitly that the campaign faced an “overwhelming wave of Chinese intervention” and called on Beijing to stop its citizens from interfering in the election. Fourth-ranked KMT chairman candidate Chang Ya-chung similarly claimed to have discovered at least ten “virtual anchor” channels from the PRC commenting on the KMT election and favoring a “single candidate.”[54] He alleged that the candidate’s team was using foreign resources to attack opponents. Hau, Jaw, and Chang did not specify which candidate they believed benefited from the intervention, but Chang provided a screenshot of a video that mentioned Cheng Li-wun, and Hau used a feminine pronoun [妳] that likewise implied Cheng, the only female candidate in the race.[55] Cheng’s campaign denied the implicit allegations and said that they lacked evidence.[56] The PRC Taiwan Affairs Office also dismissed the allegations, saying that “the comments of some mainland netizens do not reflect the official position.”[57]
Key Takeaways
- PRC military support to Russia: PRC manufacturers have dramatically increased fiber optic drone component exports to Russia, possibly indicating a heightened PRC commitment to Russian battlefield success in Ukraine.
- US-PRC trade disputes: The PRC expanded its export controls over rare earths ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, highlighting how it uses its market dominance for economic coercion and to disrupt the international flow of critical resources.
- Taiwan Kuomintang (KMT) chairperson election: Former KMT legislator Cheng Li-wun won the KMT chairperson election, defeating the establishment favorite Hau Lung-bin. Cheng is a vocal advocate for a shared “Chinese” identity among Taiwanese people.
- Inter-Korean dynamics: South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young confirmed that the Lee administration will pursue a two-state framework for inter-Korean relations, moving away from the long-standing South Korea policy endorsing unification.
Cross-Strait Relations
Taiwan
The Taiwanese military is moving toward an asymmetric defense strategy while balancing its commitment to conventional systems. The Taiwanese military is also showing positive signs of learning from foreign conflicts. Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense released its biannual National Defense Report on October 9, outlining Taiwan’s strategic priorities.[58] The report presented Taiwan’s strategy as “Resilient Defense and Multi-Domain Deterrence” that emphasized the Taiwanese commitment to enhancing asymmetric warfare capabilities.[59] An asymmetric defense of Taiwan would attempt to leverage the island’s inherent defensive advantages of rough terrain and limited landing areas while taking steps to mitigate the PLA advantage in manpower, advanced equipment, and precision strike capabilities. A force tailored for asymmetric defense would prioritize decentralized command, mobile firepower, and a high volume of low-cost systems.[60] The Ministry of National Defense will prioritize improving mobile anti-ship and anti-air batteries and procuring drones in large quantities to further its asymmetric defense.[61] The report stated that these priorities are reflected in the largest-ever special budget request for “strengthening defense resilience and asymmetric capability program procurement” that includes funding for improving Taiwan’s air defense network, drone detection capabilities, and domestic arms production.[62] Taiwan’s Legislative Yuan (LY) must approve the special budget before it goes into effect.
The report also stressed intended improvements to Taiwan’s reserve forces. Reserve forces would likely play an important role in an asymmetric defense of Taiwan by providing frontline and rear area support to Taiwan’s regular forces.[63] The report outlined enhanced training for reserve forces focused on incorporating unmanned systems and simulating the defense of coastlines, urban areas, and infrastructure.[64] The report stated that reserve forces must be rapidly mobilized and capable of fighting independently or in conjunction with regular forces in the event of a contingency.[65] Heightened emphasis on reserve force training and deployment reflects lessons learned from the critical role Ukraine’s Territorial Defense Forces played in the early months of Russia’s war in Ukraine.[66]
The report maintained a strong focus on conventional equipment, such as the M1AT2 Abrams main battle tank, F-16V fighter aircraft, and the Patriot air-defense system.[67] The Taiwanese Navy is also moving forward with plans to construct two light frigates in 2026 which replaced a previous plan to procure several dozen smaller missile boats for coastal defense.[68] The prioritization of these systems reflects a bifurcated emphasis in the report that balances asymmetric capabilities with conventional, exquisite systems. Such conventional systems would likely be vulnerable to a PLA first strike against the island in the event of an invasion. High-end conventional systems, such as the light frigate project and Taiwan’s indigenous submarine project, remain important for countering PRC coercion, however.[69]
Taiwan is taking concrete steps to incorporate asymmetry into its air defense strategy. Taiwanese President William Lai Ching-te announced the “T-Dome” multi-layered air defense concept during his National Day speech on October 10.[70] Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo said that the layered air defense network would feature closer “sensor-to-shooter” system integration, allowing Taiwan’s air defenses to achieve higher success rates when intercepting threats, while also allocating resources more efficiently. Koo stressed the importance of integrating anti-air, anti-missile, and anti-drone defenses and said that Taiwan would “prioritize procurement that emphasizes mobility and high survivability.”[71] These priorities parallel the 2025 National Defense Report’s focus on cost-effective systems that can survive a PLA first strike.
Taiwan’s planned air defense concept also appears to incorporate lessons learned from recent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. Multi-layered integrated air and missile defense (IAMD) networks have proven highly effective at defeating large-scale missile and drone attacks, which Taiwan would likely face in a PRC invasion.[72] Investment in an IAMD network would increase the survivability of Taiwanese systems and reduce the effectiveness of large-scale PLA missile strike campaigns. Taiwan’s procurement priorities likely indicate its desire to bring its forces in line with stated US desires for a Taiwanese asymmetric defense strategy, while still investing in more exquisite systems.
Taiwan’s energy sector remains highly vulnerable to a PRC short-of-war blockade campaign. Taiwan’s supplemental budget proposal for economic, social, and defense resilience dedicated funding to energy resilience. The Wall Street Journal released a report on October 7, citing a wargame led by the US think tank Foundation for the Defense of Democracies, that suggested a PRC blockade of Taiwan would deplete the island’s liquified natural gas (LNG) reserves in 11 days.[73] The US think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies also concluded a series of wargames in July 2025 that showed that Taiwan’s electricity production would fall to around 20 percent of its current capacity on week eight of a PRC blockade, crippling the island’s economy.[74] Approximately 97 percent of Taiwan’s energy is imported from overseas.[75]
Taiwan’s Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin addressed concerns surrounding Taiwan’s energy security on October 9. Kung vowed to expand Taiwan’s energy reserves “as quickly as possible” to prevent swift capitulation in the event of a PRC blockade.[76] Kung also said that Taiwan could lean on coal-fired energy plants, hydropower, and other renewable energy sources to offset negative effects from a blockade.[77]
The LY passed the special budget for social, economic, and defense resilience on October 17 that includes funds for emergency energy purchases that would improve Taiwan’s ability to withstand a PRC blockade.[78] Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo told the LY on October 8 that the special budget earmarked 3.2 billion New Taiwan Dollars (104 million US dollars) for “war-preparedness fuel” purchases and dispersed storage to increase Taiwan’s resilience.[79] The special budget for resilience intends to expand Taiwan’s wartime reserves of critical supplies to last 120 days without resupply during a contingency.[80] Taiwan’s energy imports will likely remain vulnerable to PRC interdiction, however, particularly as Taiwan continues to shut down its domestic nuclear power facilities.
The PRC released two reward notices for Taiwanese military officers and military intelligence officers, respectively, and accused them of “secessionist” activity. This likely marks a new PRC cognitive warfare effort to spread concern within the Taiwanese military, government, and populace over the levels of PRC infiltration within the Taiwanese military. The PRC Ministry of State Security issued a bounty for three individuals identified as lieutenant colonels in the Taiwanese Military Intelligence Bureau (MIB) on October 10.[81] The ministry accused the individuals of conducting propaganda and sabotage efforts, spreading pro-independence messages, and inciting cross-strait tensions online, in violation of the PRC’s Anti-Secession Law. The Xiamen Public Security Bureau issued a reward notice on October 11 for 18 Taiwanese military officers alleged to be members of a “psychological warfare” unit conducting “secessionist” activities online.[82] The notice offered a 10,000 yuan (1,400 US dollars) reward for information leading to the capture of the identified officers.
The Taiwanese Ministry of National Defense called the PRC’s accusations an “act of cognitive warfare” intended to divide public opinion and undermine the Taiwanese government.[83] The PRC previously accused 20 individuals from the Ministry of National Defense Information, Communication, and Electronic Force Command (ICEFCOM) of “Taiwanese-Independence” activity in June, following an alleged DPP-ordered cyberattack against a PRC tech company.[84] The PRC notices included names, identification numbers, and pictures of those accused of “secessionist” activity, stating that the information was provided by “concerned Taiwanese citizens.”[85] These bounty announcements are unlikely to lead to arrests of the Taiwanese individuals, as Taiwanese military officers rarely travel to the PRC. The PRC is likely pursuing a new line of cognitive warfare targeting the Taiwanese military and general populace. The notices’ inclusion of personal information of those accused suggests high levels of infiltration within the Taiwanese military and military intelligence apparatuses. This could lead to diminished public trust in the Taiwanese military and diminished trust and security within the Taiwanese military.
PRC methods for recruitment of Taiwanese agents to conduct espionage focus on exploiting financial vulnerability in military personnel. Taiwan indicted two Taiwanese military personnel for leaking secrets to the PRC on October 12.[86] An undercover PRC intelligence operative recruited a discharged Taiwanese navy private, surnamed Lin, to act as an agent of the PRC in 2023, after his expulsion from the military. Lin, in turn, recruited an active-duty soldier to provide sensitive military information to the PRC, including the manual to Taiwan’s Hsiung Feng II anti-ship missile, in return for approximately 1,200 USD.
This espionage case illustrates the four primary methods that the PRC uses to build spy networks in Taiwan, as outlined by the National Security Bureau (NSB): using retired military personnel to recruit active-duty personnel, contacting targets through online means, using financial inducements, and exploiting targets’ indebtedness to coerce them.[87] Taiwan has prosecuted 24 people for spying for the PRC since the start of 2025, over half of which were retired or current military personnel.[88]
Taiwanese Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo said on October 13 that the military will strengthen the screening of military personnel who have access to sensitive information to shield Taiwan from the PRC’s pervasive infiltration efforts.[89]
The PRC espionage efforts extend beyond the recruitment of military personnel. A manager from EVA Air, a Taiwanese airline, confessed on October 14 to acting as an agent of the PRC since 2014.[90] The manager attempted to bribe a junior employee at Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council, the primary agency responsible for conducting cross-strait relations, to provide sensitive information to the PRC.[91] The employee refused, however.
China
The PRC is continuing efforts to reduce its reliance on US chips by enforcing the ban of advanced Nvidia chips and bolstering its own domestic production. The Financial Times reported that the PRC is conducting strict customs checks on semiconductor imports to enforce the Cyberspace Administration of China’s (CAC) ban of Nvidia H20 and RTX Pro 6000D processors.[92] The United States had leveraged access to Nvidia H20 chips in trade negotiations during the summer of 2025. The CAC’s ban was in response to US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s July 15 remarks on wanting PRC developers “addicted to the American technology stack.”[93] The PRC, in response, made plans to triple its chip production in 2026. PRC tech company Huawei publicly announced in September 2025 its plans to double its chip production in 2026 compared to 2025; this is unusual as the three-year plan is typically not publicized.[94]
Ministry of Commerce announced on October 9 that 14 foreign organizations were added to its “unreliable entity list.”[95] The PRC also launched an antimonopoly investigation against Qualcomm on October 10.[96] The PRC is also probing Nvidia for antimonopoly and announced preliminary findings that Nvidia was guilty during the Madrid trade talks in September.[97] The PRC appears to be utilizing its regulatory power to limit American influence in the chips industry.
Northeast Asia
Japan
The Japanese Ministry of Defense announced that the Japan Self Defense Force (JSDF) will conduct its annual joint exercise in areas where PRC and Russian military vessels and aircraft have been frequently spotted. The JSDF plans to conduct anti-ship and missile defense drills near Hokkaido, Kyushu, and the Southwestern Islands.[98] The JSDF will also conduct exercises focused on airborne operations, runway repair, logistics, electronic warfare, communications, and amphibious/anti-amphibious operations in Okinawa. Approximately 55 US military personnel will participate in a combined command post training to enhance joint command capability and interoperability.
The planned exercises likely reflect Japan’s growing concerns about the PRC’s increased activity in the East China Sea. In addition to the joint exercise Japan has also demonstrated its commitment to strengthening its southwestern defense system by deploying additional missiles in September and conducting a rare minelaying exercise around the Sakishima Islands, approximately 100km from Taiwan, on October 3, 2025.[99]
The PRC has not commented on the exercise at the time of writing. While the PRC frequently criticizes Japan’s efforts to enhance its defense capabilities and has warned Japan to “act prudently in the military security field,” it has rarely commented on the JSDF’s routine unilateral exercises, however.[100] The PRC usually reserves its criticisms for JSDF’s exercises with foreign countries for destabilizing regional security.[101]
North Korea
Worker’s Party of Korea (WPK) General Secretary Kim Jong Un met with leaders from Laos and Vietnam between October 7 and 10 during their visits to mark the 80th anniversary of the founding of the WPK. Laotian President Thongloun Sisoulith held talks with Kim on October 7 at the WPK Central Committee headquarters, where both sides agreed to further develop their “traditional friendly and cooperative relationship.”[102] Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) General Secretary To Lam also met with Kim on October 9. To praised North Korea’s “eye-opening success” in “rejuvenating itself through self-reliance” and affirmed the CPV’s commitment to “further consolidate the traditional relations of friendship” with the WPK.[103] North Korea and Vietnam signed multiple agreements on October 10 covering cooperation in areas including defense, health care, culture, media, aviation, judicial assistance, investment and avoiding double taxation for their citizens.
North Korea appears to be broadening its diplomatic outreach beyond its traditional allies, the PRC and Russia, by deepening ties with long-standing socialist partners such as Laos and Vietnam. North Korea resumed diplomatic engagement with Laos and Vietnam after a period of hiatus during the COVID-19 pandemic shutdown by dispatching a delegation led by Director of the International Department of the WPK Kim Song Nam to both countries in March 2024.[104] A Vietnamese military delegation visited in September 2024, and a Laotian delegation led by Laos’ Deputy Foreign Minister visited North Korea in March 2025.
Vietnam played an intermediary role between the United States and North Korea in 2019 by hosting a bilateral summit in Hanoi, in line with its emphasis on maintaining regional stability for economic development. North Korea’s efforts to accelerate diplomatic engagement with Vietnam also appears to go beyond economic exchanges, aiming to increase its influence within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) through its partnership with Vietnam. Kim has increasingly stressed North Korea’s need for a more active international role following his attendance at Beijing’s September 3 Victory Day parade, suggesting that closer ties with Moscow and Beijing are emboldening Pyongyang’s diplomatic ambitions.
PRC Premier Li Qiang visited North Korea to commemorate the WPK’s 80th anniversary, signaling greatly improved bilateral relations following a downturn since 2020. This was the first visit of a PRC premier to North Korea since 2009.[105] Li held talks with Kim on October 9, reaffirming Beijing’s “unwavering policy” of strengthening ties with Pyongyang and called for closer coordination in promoting a “more just and equitable” international order.[106] The discussion focused on expanding high-level exchanges and enhancing strategic communication between the two countries.[107] Li held additional talks with North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song on October 11, during which Pak expressed North Korea’s support for PRC policies on Taiwan and emphasized the need for joint opposition to “hegemonism,” a word regularly invoked by both countries to criticize US influence in the international system.[108]
Li’s visit demonstrates the normalization of bilateral relations following Kim’s summit with Xi at the September 3 Victory Day parade in Beijing. Signs of renewed bilateral relations emerged at the beginning of 2025, highlighted by the return of PRC journalists to Pyongyang and the resumption of construction on border customs facilities near the New Yalu River.[109] CDOT-ISW assessed this surge as the PRC’s attempt to regain influence over North Korea, counterbalancing Russia’s growing role in Pyongyang.
The two countries are also seeking closer coordination on the international stage, deepening their strategic alignment against the United States based on the PRC’s new global governance framework. CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping announced the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) on September 2, which promotes an alternative international order led by the PRC.[110] North Korea has voiced its support for the initiative, possibly to leverage the GGI framework to reinforce its longstanding characterization of the United States as a destabilizing force in the region and further justify its nuclear build-up as “self-defense.” Kim’s emphasis on coordination within multilateral platforms likely aims to help build resilience against international sanctions.
A Russian delegation led by the leader of the ruling United Russia party, Dmitry Medvedev, visited North Korea on October 9, further deepening military and diplomatic ties between the two countries. Medvedev met with WPK Secretary Jo Yong Won and issued a joint statement expressing Russia’s support for North Korea’s efforts to bolster its defense capabilities. The statement cited “mounting political and military tension on the Eurasian continent” resulting from “the aggressive politics of the West.”[111] Medvedev held talks with Kim on October 10, during which Kim emphasized the importance of strengthening “political coordination” between the two countries to create a “favorable political environment” for the development of bilateral relations.[112] Medvedev also highlighted the role of North Korean troops in supporting Russian operations in the Kursk region. The Seoul-based news outlet NK News identified an additional 25 top Russian military and party officials who traveled with Medvedev to mark North Korea’s Party foundation Day anniversary.[113]
The large Russian delegation to North Korea highlights a strong continuity in deepening diplomatic and military cooperation between the two countries since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea had transferred over nine million rounds of mixed artillery shells and ammunition to Russia by 2024 and dispatched approximately 14,000 North Korean troops to support Russian operations in Kursk Oblast since October 2024.[114] Russia, in exchange, has eased its stance on international sanctions against North Korea at the United Nations Security Council and has reportedly transferred weapons and technology to support North Korea’s arms development, including at least one Pantsir-class air defense system.[115] North Korea displayed a new short-range air defense system that resembles Russia’s Pantsir-S1 at its annual Defense Development Exhibition on October 5.[116] The two countries have continued high-level exchanges, highlighted by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to Pyongyang in June 2024 and Kim’s summit with Putin on the sidelines of the September 3 Victory Day parade in Beijing. Russia and North Korea are aligning in their anti-Western narrative, blaming “aggressive politics by the West” for tensions in the region and the globe in an October 10 joint statement.[117]
South Korea
The Lee Jae Myung administration is trying to secure support from the United States and the PRC for its proposal to denuclearize the Korean Peninsula. The PRC is unlikely to endorse the proposal and appears to have become more tolerant of North Korea’s nuclear program. South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoonjoo and US Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Alison Hooker reaffirmed their shared commitment to the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula at a strategic dialogue on October 10. Park explained the Lee administration’s proposed denuclearization roadmap, while Hooker emphasized the importance of the US, South Korean, and Japanese trilateral cooperation.[118] South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun also urged Beijing’s support for the administration’s denuclearization objective during a phone call with the PRC Foreign Minister Wang Yi earlier on October 7. Wang Yi emphasized the PRC’s efforts to promote regional peace and stability but did not directly address North Korean.[119] CDOT-ISW has previously assessed that the PRC may have softened its past opposition to North Korea’s nuclear program, following CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping’s unprecedented omission of the issue during his meeting with Kim Jong Un on September 5.[120]
The Lee administration has prioritized restoring inter-Korean dialogue, aiming to reduce North Korean nuclear threat, and ultimately achieve denuclearization based on its three-step E.N.D. (Exchange, Normalization, Denuclearization) roadmap.[121] Pyongyang has explicitly refused to engage with Seoul or to discuss denuclearization, however.[122] PRC and Russian support have emboldened North Korea and could make dialogue on denuclearization difficult in the foreseeable future.
Southeast Asia
Philippines
The PRC may be escalating its attempts to block Philippine resupply missions to fishermen around the South China Sea, including near Thitu Island, the administrative center for Philippine territory in the Spratly archipelago. Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Jay Tarriela reported that China Coast Guard (CCG) ships carried out “dangerous and provocative maneuvers” against three Philippine Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessels anchored in the territorial waters of Thitu Island on October 12.[123] Thitu Island is the administrative center for the Philippines’ Spratly Islands territories and the site of a Philippine military outpost.[124] Tarriela said that CCG ships blasted water cannons at the BFAR ships and that one of the CCG vessels, CCG 21559, rammed the BFAR ship Datu Pagbuaya and caused minor damage.[125] The CCG released its own statement blaming Datu Pagbuaya for ignoring warnings and “dangerously approach[ing]” CCG 21559 as it was carrying out “normal law enforcement operations.” [126] CCG and PCG videos both showed the CCG ship colliding with Datu Pagbuaya from behind, however.[127] The CCG also claimed that two of the BFAR ships had “intruded” into the waters of nearby Sandy Cay, an unoccupied reef platform.[128] The PRC and the Philippines both claim the Spratly Islands as their territory.
The PRC has occasionally tried to block or expel Philippine missions around Thitu Island in recent years, but usually focuses on contesting Philippine presence in places where the Philippines is less entrenched, such as Second Thomas Shoal and Scarborough Shoal. The recent confrontation may be a sign of renewed PRC interest in contesting maritime control around Thitu. CDOT-ISW observed a PRC research ship conducting likely seabed mapping operations around Thitu Island and Sandy Cay on October 7, several days before this incident.[129] Sandy Cay is one of the only contested features where both PRC and Philippine personnel have landed to conduct scientific research or raise flags.[130] Sandy Cay is legally significant as a “rock” that generates twelve nautical miles of territorial waters for whichever state owns it.[131] The radius of Sandy Cay’s territorial waters could give the controlling state a claim to nearby Subi Reef, the site of a large PRC naval base, which is an artificial island that does not have its own territorial waters.
The PRC may be attempting to disrupt the Philippine strategy of using fishing boats to maintain a presence in Philippine-claimed waters. The PRC also tried to block Philippine resupply missions to fishermen near Scarborough Shoal and Sabina Shoal from October 8-13.[132] Tarriela said that the PCG and BFAR delivered fuel subsidies, food, and crushed ice to over 50 fishing boats at Scarborough Shoal and over 40 at Sabina Shoal, despite blocking maneuvers and harassment from over twenty CCG, Chinese Maritime Militia (CMM), and PLA Navy vessels at each location.[133]
The PRC is using its new “nature reserve” at Scarborough Shoal to justify blocking the resupply of Philippine fishing boats. The PRC declared a new “nature reserve” over part of Scarborough Shoal on September 9.[134] PCG spokesperson Tarriela reported that CCG broadcasts referenced this “nature reserve” for the first time as justification for blocking Philippine resupply missions on October 13, claiming that Philippine fishing boats could damage the nature reserve.[135] The PRC likely established this “nature reserve” to give it more legal justification for aggressive action against Philippine vessels, as ship tracking data shows that PRC fishing boats continue to operate in the area unobstructed.
Russia
The US Department of Transportation proposed a ban on Chinese airlines flying over Russian airspace to the United States, likely to impose costs on the PRC for its role in supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine. The department announced a tentative ban that would apply to flights from PRC airlines Air China, China Eastern, Xiamen Airlines, and China Southern traveling to the United States on October 9.[136] The department stated that, because these airlines can fly through Russian airspace, their flights are shorter and cheaper than US competitors.[137] Russia banned US and European airlines from its airspace in 2022 in retaliation for Western sanctions over its invasion of Ukraine. The proposed US ban would prevent passenger flights and “combination services” that transport passengers, cargo, and mail from flying through Russian airspace on the way to the United States.[138] PRC Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun denounced the potential ban, stating that the United States should consider the domestic implications before seeking to “suppress” other nations.[139] The proposed ban would come into effect in early November.[140]
Israel/Palestine
The PRC voiced approval of the Israel-Hamas ceasefire while promoting its own longer-term resolution to the conflict. PRC Foreign Affairs Minister Wang Yi stated on October 10 that the PRC welcomes any effort to restore peace and save lives in response to the first phase of the ceasefire, which began on October 8.[141] Wang said that the PRC’s three necessary conditions to resolve the conflict are to achieve a lasting ceasefire and alleviate the humanitarian crisis, restore the governance of the Gaza Strip to Palestinians, and work toward a two-state solution and the creation of a Palestinian state.[142] The PRC has consistently urged the international community to support its three conditions and characterized the United States’ role in the conflict as “inflammatory” due to its support for Israel.[143] The PRC has worked to accrue international support for its position on the war, including issuing several joint statements on the conflict with several Arab states.[144]
PRC official media avoided acknowledging the United States’ role in brokering the ceasefire and characterized the peace summit in Egypt on October 13 as a US political stunt that failed to address concrete steps to peace.[145] A failed ceasefire would provide the PRC with another opportunity to gain support for its own peace proposals and further present itself as a global mediator.
Iran
Note: a version of the following text appeared in the ISW-CTP Iran Update on October 15.
The PRC continues to receive Iranian oil exports at Chinese port terminals despite five rounds of US sanctions that have targeted Chinese port terminals and oil refineries for receiving illicit Iranian crude oil.[146] Trading firms diverted at least six crude oil tankers from a crude oil import terminal in Shandong Province that the United States sanctioned on October 9 to other eastern Chinese port terminals, according to shipping data and trading sources who spoke to Reuters on October 13 and 15.[147] PRC MFA Spokesperson Guo Jiakun defended the PRC’s “normal cooperation” with Iran on October 10 and criticized “illegal unilateral sanctions.”[148] The PRC continues to repudiate US sanctions against Iranian energy exports by accepting the ships at other terminals.[149] The PRC imports around 90 percent of Iranian crude oil exports, which remain an economic lifeline for Iran amid increased Western sanctions.[150] Shandong Province port authorities have issued notices previously banning terminal operators from receiving US-sanctioned or non-registered vessels, but these notices have had limited effects.[151] These notices have not directly impacted the PRC’s ability to offload Iranian oil exports because sanctioned vessels carrying Iranian crude oil conduct ship-to-ship transfers with non-sanctioned vessels that then offload at Chinese ports.[152] Iranian oil exports to the PRC have remained high, averaging 1.8 million barrels per day in the first half of 2025, despite US President Donald Trump’s second round of “maximum pressure” campaign sanctions that seek to drive Iranian oil exports to zero.[153]

docs.title: KMT Cheng Li - wun urges broader TPP collaboration
docs.snippet: Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) yesterday called on Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) to broade...
docs.content:
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) yesterday called on Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) Chairman Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) to broaden election and policy collaboration at a summit of the two party leaders in New Taipei City.
The KMT and TPP over the past year have deepened their collaboration from elections to the local level in a milestone of the nation’s democratic development, Cheng told a news conference.
The two parties should continue working together in elections for commissioners, mayors and local government councils to avoid competition that benefits the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), she said.
Photo: Wang Yi-song, Taipei Times
The opposition’s collaboration should be directed with an eye to aligning politics with the wishes of the public, which means the most immediately popular candidate should not necessarily obtain the leadership’s backing, Cheng said.
The KMT-TPP alliance’s main challenge is to win the local elections next year to ensure the continued survival of core democratic values and promote the opposition’s policies, she said.
The opposition parties must carve out a new path for their alliance by recognizing that their responsibility takes precedence over self-interest and that missteps of the past are not repeated.
Cheng said that she had little previous dealings with Huang, but is confident that the two share a common vision and belief about the future of the coalition.
The KMT and TPP’s collaboration would have to take a unique form, as Taiwan’s system of government is not fully presidential or parliamentary, she said, apparently referring to Huang’s comments suggesting the opposition strive to form coalition governments.
Asked whether the two parties have achieved a consensus regarding their China policy, Huang said that establishing foundational values and objectives would be more important than policy.
The DPP’s stance on Taiwanese independence is less important than finding ways to truly defend Taiwan’s way of life, Huang said.
Additional reporting by Shi Hsiao-kuang and Lin Che-yuan

docs.title: Autumn Struggle  marchers slam Lai NT$1 . 25 trillion defense plan
docs.snippet: Taipei, Nov. 30 (CNA) Around 200 people marched in Taipei on Sunday in the annual "Autumn Struggle" protest, criticizing President Lai Ching-te's (賴清德...
docs.content:
Taipei, Nov. 30 (CNA) Around 200 people marched in Taipei on Sunday in the annual "Autumn Struggle" protest, criticizing President Lai Ching-te's (賴清德) proposed NT$1.25 trillion (US$39.85 billion) supplementary defense budget and urging the government to prioritize social welfare spending.
Traditionally one of Taiwan's main labor demonstrations, but now encompassing broader social issues, the event began outside the Legislative Yuan with speeches on labor rights, opposition to war and objections to Taiwan's growing defense outlays.
At the rally on Ketagalan Boulevard, opposition Kuomintang Chairperson Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) accused the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) of neglecting workers while treating large-scale military procurement as routine.
"Taiwanese workers have been stuck in a deep winter for many years, yet they have not received even a glance of concern from those in power," she said, arguing that Lai's proposed NT$1.25 trillion plan, covering arms purchases and joint development projects with the United States from 2026 to 2033, risked inflaming cross-strait tensions rather than easing them.
Protest organizer Lin Tzu-wen (林子文) estimated the turnout at about 200 people.
Among the participants was Chen Hung-pei (陳虹霈) of the People Democracy Party, who argued that expanding arms spending by "such a large amount" primarily served U.S. interests and diverted funds from groups in need.
For example, she said, Taiwan's long-term care system only provides about three hours of daily home-care services to people with muscular atrophy.
"This is far from enough," she said, adding that if just a "fraction" of the NT$1.25 trillion -- about NT$200 billion -- were redirected to the long-term care budget, "it could instead allow them to receive nine hours of care a day."
The DPP did not directly respond to the demands raised at the event, but issued a statement around the time of the rally rejecting Cheng's criticisms.
In the face of China's continued military pressure, the DPP said, Taiwan has a responsibility to "be prepared for war without seeking war," a principle it said has guided the government from former President Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) to Lai.

docs.title: Donovan Deep Dives : President Lai big bucks defense budget blitz
docs.snippet: This week, President William Lai (賴清德) and his administration launched a major publicity blitz to drum up support for a proposed NT$1.25 trillion (US$...
docs.content:
This week, President William Lai (賴清德) and his administration launched a major publicity blitz to drum up support for a proposed NT$1.25 trillion (US$40 billion) special defense budget. This was well-planned and executed, and politically astute, but it is still far from becoming a reality: He needs to convince the opposition-controlled legislature to pass it.
The chance that the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) legislative caucuses vote to approve everything that the administration wants is low, but Lai and his team have gone to great lengths to optimize the chances of getting some, or even most of it, passed.
The president kicked things off with a piece entitled “Taiwan’s president: I will boost defense spending to protect our democracy” in the <
Photo: AFP
He followed this hours later with a major speech entitled “National Security Action Plan to Safeguard Democratic Taiwan.”
AMERICA BACKS LAI
As Taiwan’s primary military backer, Taiwanese pay close attention to what is being said and reported about the nation in Washington, and Lai played to this very effectively. If he had launched this domestically first, it would have been given less coverage locally, and it would have likely only reached the outside world in dribs and drabs.
Photo: AFP
Getting American support increases the pressure on the opposition to pass this legislation. The Taiwanese public is broadly pro-American and acutely aware that they are economically and militarily dependent on the superpower
Lai’s piece was well-written to appeal to American officials. As is now customary, it is full of praise for US President Donald Trump’s leadership, and included the line, “The international community is safer today because of the Trump administration’s pursuit of peace through strength.”
Responding to repeated calls from within the Trump administration for Taiwan to boost defense spending, he outlined his proposals and stated: “My message here is clear: Taiwan’s dedication to peace and stability is unwavering. No country will be more determined in safeguarding Taiwan’s future than our own.”
Photo: Reuters
This was swiftly backed up by a strongly supportive social media post by American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) Director Raymond Greene, giving Lai’s proposals a public American stamp of approval.
Though AIT is normally careful about intervening in local politics, Greene openly put his thumb on the scale by saying, “Just as support for Taiwan is a longstanding US bipartisan priority, I expect Taiwan’s political parties will find similar common ground.”
Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) also weighed in by stating that “preliminary negotiations were complete” on the entire plan and timeline for the budget proposal with the US Department of War. This, plus Greene’s swift response, suggests that the Americans are fully aware and on board with Lai’s plans, and are willing to spend political capital to put pressure on the legislature to pass it.
Photo: AFP
SWEETENING THE POT
The full details of the proposal to be sent to the legislature are not yet finalized, but from what is known, it appears that public opinion, constituent buy-in and blunting expected potential KMT criticisms were all carefully considered.
Emphasis has been placed on what is being termed variously as “Taiwan Dome” or “T-Dome.” This concept is partially inspired by Israel’s “Iron Dome” missile defense systems. This plan was previously announced, but more details are coming out.
Lai described it this way: “I am also accelerating the development of ‘T-Dome,’ a multilayered, integrated defense system designed to protect Taiwan from PRC missiles, rockets, drones, and combat aircraft. Together with other AI-driven and unmanned platforms, these capabilities bring us closer to the vision of an unassailable Taiwan, safeguarded by innovation and technology.”
Lai wants to “vastly enhance Taiwan’s asymmetrical capabilities” to make this happen. This is something Washington has been calling for.
This also appears to sidestep one of the biggest criticisms from skeptics in the KMT, that Taiwan is wasting money on flashy, big-ticket items like fighter jets that can play an offensive attack role, which they consider to be “provocative” to Beijing.
A defensive system designed to protect Taiwan from incoming attack, based on a multitude of smaller systems, is an easier sell to the public and the KMT.
Additionally, Lai also emphasized building up the local defense supply chain as part of the project, creating wealth and jobs domestically in the process, not just serving as an “ATM” for the Americans. This could also benefit constituents of opposition lawmakers.
The entire budget is also not as impressive as the headlines suggest, as it is spread out over eight years, and may or may not include already budgeted items for next year. To put the sum in perspective, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.’s (TSMC) projected capital expenditures for next year alone are US$48 to 50 billion, significantly bigger than this entire eight-year special budget.
The president has also emphasized that Taiwan’s defense spending will reach 5 percent of GDP by 2030, but this special budget likely will not get Taiwan there alone. More likely, the plan is to follow the new NATO standards, with 3.5 percent on traditional “hard” defense spending and 1.5 percent on infrastructure that could serve a military purpose in war — potentially opening up more juicy budgets for opposition lawmakers’ districts that can be negotiated over.
Further signalling that they expect negotiations with opposition parties, Defense Minister Koo described the entire budget as the “upper limit” of what they hope to spend.
This has been thought out to maximize public pressure to pass a special budget, while leaving enough negotiating room and potential goodies for opposition lawmakers to make passing at least some of it palatable.
BUT WILL THEY BITE?
This puts the KMT in a tough spot. Earlier this year, former KMT Chairman Eric Chu (朱立倫) called for defense spending to be raised to 3.5 percent of GDP.
Current Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) has only been in office since Nov. 1, and she comes from the most pro-China, US-skeptic wing of the party. Her firebrand stances won her the chair race, but with only half of the votes in an election limited to party members and with a very low turnout.
Lai has backed Cheng into a corner; if she fights against this too hard, she risks alienating voters ahead of the 2026 local elections. Her ideology plays well to the base, but average KMT supporters are far more moderate, and to win elections, the party needs to appeal to the even more moderate mainstream independents.
True to form, Cheng has come out guns blazing against the plan, even using a term popular with Chinese state media, saying Lai is “playing with fire.” She also criticized the plan saying, “Taiwan should not be an ammunition dump and weapons factory.”
However, it is too soon to know how much authority she has within the party. KMT legislative caucus convener Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) has echoed some of her language, but has not entirely ruled it out.
Perhaps even more importantly, the KMT’s most popular politician and frontrunner to become the party’s presidential candidate in 2028, Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) has taken a far more moderate tone.
She emphasized that supporting the military and national defense are necessary, but also stressed legislative oversight to ensure taxpayer money is not wasted and the funds are spent appropriately.
Fu and the KMT legislative caucus so far have leaned more hardline, but nowhere near as far as Cheng. Last year, they orchestrated significant cuts to the administration’s planned increases to the military budget, but in the end, it was still a record-high budget — and ahead of this year’s recall votes, they rolled back most of the sections of the budget that they had frozen.
Fu may be hardline, but he is less of an ideologue and more interested in winning elections and getting his home county of Hualian big budgets. He may be more open to negotiation than Cheng, but it is unclear whether he is willing to buck her as party leader or buck the presumed next party leader, Lu.
This is Cheng’s first big test, and it will likely be revealing as to how much power she really holds in the party.
It will also be a revealing test for TPP Chairman and caucus convener Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌). In the 2024 presidential election, TPP founder and then-presidential candidate Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) talked strong on defense, sometimes even sounding more hawkish than the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and Lai.
It would be a big risk for Huang — who is currently in Japan — to contradict Ko’s stances, which remain unchanged as the party’s official ideology.
However, if the KMT caucus takes a hard line, Huang and the TPP would be taking a big risk in defying senior partners in their coalition, which is currently negotiating which party’s candidates will run unopposed by the other party in next year’s elections.
That could put Huang in a tough spot.
So far, Huang has taken a moderate stance, saying in a video message that the TPP supports a “reasonable” increase in defense spending, but would conduct a “practical and rational” review to ensure taxpayers’ money is well spent.

China-Japan clash may persist a year, Taiwan minister warns
Sign up now: Get insights on Asia's fast-moving developments
Follow topic:
TAIPEI – The dispute between China and Japan could drag on for a year, Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said, adding Taipei hoped the two sides could find a way to resolve their differences.
In a Bloomberg News interview on Dec 2, Mr Lin said the tensions sparked by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s comments
He added that worsening the friction or issues related to Taiwan would offer little benefit to any party.
“For Beijing, it’s also not in its interest to escalate the conflict,” Mr Lin added in his first TV interview with the foreign media since taking up the diplomatic post in 2024.
The Foreign Ministry in Beijing did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Taiwan is at the centre of the dispute between China and Japan, which started after Ms Takaichi commented on the possible involvement of Japanese troops if China were to invade Taiwan.
Beijing saw those remarks as crossing a red line, and responded with economic and diplomatic reprisals – though Ms Takaichi has rebuffed its demand to retract the remarks.
Taiwan’s response to the episode has been fairly muted, with Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te urging Beijing to act like a responsible major power, an apparent reference to Beijing’s retaliatory moves.
Mr Lin has also encouraged Taiwanese travellers to visit Japan and buy the nation’s goods – a contrast to the wave of cancellations from China
He reiterated that backing for Japan in the interview on Dec 2, saying that “we show our support through, I think, a soft approach” while also trying “to help cool down the situation”.
He also said that Taiwan “brought together representatives from like-minded countries” to discuss the spat over Ms Takaichi’s remarks.
Though he did not name any countries, Taipei often says it maintains close communication with the US, its main military backer.
Mr Lin added that “we also communicated with various countries through our established channels both before and after the spat broke out, and there is a solid foundation of mutual trust”.
Officials in Taipei “have no doubt on the Trump administration’s commitment to the regional security in the Indo-Pacific”, Mr Lin said in the interview.
There have been some questions about US President Donald Trump’s views on Taiwan, given he said while campaigning for a second term that Taipei should pay for US protection and also accused the self-governing democracy of stealing America’s chip industry.
Some other points Mr Lin mentioned in the interview:
Taipei has proposed holding a meeting in January with South African officials to resolve a dispute over the location of a Taiwanese representative office, Mr Lin said.
He added that Taipei sees “a lot of room to work with Europe,” especially on security, supply chains and defending democracy in the face of authoritarianism. Taiwanese Vice-President Hsiao Bi-khim visited Brussels in November, delivering a speech to an independent alliance of European lawmakers who advocate for a harder line on China.
Mr Lin said: “Taiwan hopes to facilitate future cooperation with the Philippines on developing (artificial intelligence) data centres.” BLOOMBERG

《TAIPEI TIMES》Lai unveils defense special budget plan
2025/10/26 03:00President William Lai attends the Taiwan Design Expo on Friday. Photo: Screen grab from the Presidential Office’s Flickr page
‘LAND VICTORY’ DRILLS: The army yesterday began its Lu Sheng 1 exercise, which focuses on participants’ proficiency in new tactics and equipment, and fighting in cities
By Jonathan Chin / Staff writer, with CNA
President William Lai （賴清德） yesterday said his administration would unveil a special budget for investing in domestic asymmetric weapons production and supply chain resilience to counter the military threat posed by China.
Lai made the remarks in a post on Facebook commemorating the Battle of Guningtou （古寧頭戰役） in 1949, saying that the nation has endured to this day because its people came together to defend it regardless of ethnicity or political opinions.
Taiwan would honor the fallen heroes from 76 years ago by providing the strongest possible support to troops serving today, he said.
Citing his address during this year’s Double Ten National Day celebrations, Lai said that the government remains committed to the defense policy priorities outlined in his speech, as well as to improving service members’ pay and living conditions.
The administration is working on a proposed “T-Dome,” a multi-layered air defense system with high detection and interception capabilities, to safeguard Taiwanese’s lives and properties, he said.
The armed forces are to integrate new technology in warfighting, including fielding drones in large numbers, forging a fast and flexible mobilization system, and maximizing the deterrence value of asymmetric capabilities, he said.
The government is soon to propose a budget for investing in asymmetric warfare capabilities and defense resilience, to create a defense industrial base capable of independently developing and mass-producing asymmetric systems, especially drones, Lai said.
The budget bill would include provisions on public-private cooperation in indigenous research and development, production at scale and securing supply chains, he said.
Under the plan, Taiwan would establish itself as a trustworthy partner for its friends and allies in joint defense industry projects, he added.
In other news, the army yesterday began its Lu Sheng 1 （陸勝, “Land Victory”） exercise, during which two combined-arms brigades would engage in simulated combat for seven days.
The drills are part of a military-wide drive to improve joint warfare capabilities, decentralize command and control, and train troops under realistic conditions, the Army Command Headquarters said.
Commanders taking part in the exercise have been instructed to sharpen the fighting skills of their units while keeping enemy capabilities in mind at all times, it added.
Lu Shen 1 focuses on participants’ proficiency in newly introduced tactics and equipment — including drones, and command and control systems — managing logistics, and fighting in cities, among other core competencies, the army said.
Additional reporting by Fang Wei-li

docs.title: Japan to seek constructive , stable ties with China : PM Takaichi
docs.snippet: Japan to seek constructive, stable ties with China: PM Takaichi (Mainichi Japan) TOKYO (Kyodo) -- Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Wednesday that Ja...
docs.content:
Japan to seek constructive, stable ties with China: PM Takaichi
(Mainichi Japan)
TOKYO (Kyodo) -- Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Wednesday that Japan will seek to build constructive and stable relations with China through dialogue amid the recent escalation of bilateral tensions.
At a press conference after an extraordinary parliamentary session ended the same day, Takaichi called China an "important neighbor," saying, "My stance of building constructive and stable relations remains unchanged since I took office."
"Japan always keeps the door open for dialogue as the two nations have issues to resolve," said Takaichi, who became the country's first female prime minister on Oct. 21 and is known for her hawkish security views.
China has taken a series of measures, including a travel advisory against visiting Japan and the resuspension of Japanese seafood imports, since Takaichi suggested on Nov. 7 that an attack on Taiwan could constitute an existential threat to Japan and warrant a response from its Self-Defense Forces.
Communist-led China views the self-ruled democratic island as a renegade province to be reunified with the mainland, by force if necessary, and sees the Taiwan issue as a purely "internal affair."
China has also been increasing its military activities. Earlier this month, Chinese fighter jets intermittently locked radar on Japanese Air Self-Defense Force aircraft in the Pacific southeast of Okinawa's main island, according to Japan's Defense Ministry.
"My remarks regarding the survival-threatening situation do not alter the stance held by the past governments," Takaichi said, adding that Japan will "persistently" explain this to China and the international community at various levels.
Her predecessors avoided discussing a specific scenario when answering questions about it.
Takaichi, meanwhile, expressed hope to hold her second in-person summit with U.S. President Donald Trump "as early as possible," while pledging to promote ties with South Korea through reciprocal visits.
In late October, Takaichi made an early diplomatic start, meeting Trump in Tokyo and holding separate talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on the sidelines of a regional gathering in South Korea.
Domestically, Takaichi's administration has struggled to manage parliamentary affairs, as the coalition of her Liberal Democratic Party and its junior partner, the Japan Innovation Party, remains a minority in the House of Councillors and holds only a slim majority in the House of Representatives.
Media polls have shown that Takaichi's Cabinet has maintained high approval ratings since its launch, and a snap general election triggered by dissolving the lower chamber could give the ruling bloc a chance to secure a comfortable majority.
At the news conference, Takaichi said that she has "no time to consider" dissolving the lower house, effectively ruling out a snap election anytime soon, and that the LDP will maintain the relationship with the JIP, known as Nippon Ishin.
The two parties signed a coalition deal on Oct. 20, helping Takaichi secure victory in a Diet vote to select the prime minister the following day.
