5 Asian Legal Business | November 2025 Keeping hearts young In 2022, Sidley launched the Built to Lead program, a first-of-its-kind partnership with Kellogg and Columbia Business Schools that equips associates and clients with MBA-level strategy and leadership training. It has been a key differentiator for lawyers that look to join and stay at Sidley and forms an important part in the firm’s DNA to develop and retain the best talent across all its offices, including associates from our Singapore office who have taken part in this award-winning program. The foundation of the program is to equip our lawyers with heightened business and boardroom literacy to evolve the role of a lawyer and enhance the value we provide to our clients. These skills allow our lawyers to be true advisors and counsel to our clients. Built to Lead also fosters collaboration and strengthens networks and relationships for associates across the Sidley platform, what for many starts as a first connection during the program evolves into cross-border work sometimes weeks and months later. At PC Woo & Co, we recognise that sustained associate engagement and retention require active investment in team bonding. We take a proactive approach and treat engagement and retention as integral components of a supportive and collaborative workplace culture, using a twist on an old cliché: we are a professional family. While making friends may not be the main objective in going to work, there is definitely a huge benefit in working with people you like and with whom you spend so much time with. Culture is key. Our firm focuses on creating meaningful connections both amongst and between teams, reaching across practice areas to help the entire firm grow closer. We have small group retreats and regular social gatherings. These bonding activities are in our firm’s DNA, and we prefer to do it organically rather than trying to formalize the process. We feel that this keeps the relationships authentic. The bonds are so strong that there are quite a few lawyers who previously left the firm yet ultimately chose to return! At a regional level, we’ve tackled this with two deliberate tracks. Regional firmwide, we host an annual regional town hall paired with a regional firm trip to bring all our colleagues together, align on strategy, and strengthen relationships. Locally, each office and in particular each practice team runs consistent, informal small-group or individual checkins. These are intentionally judgmentfree spaces where all colleagues can surface challenges, share feedback, and hear directly from leadership about the firm’s and team direction so everyone understands where we’re heading and how they fit into the growth story. We also seek and value our colleagues’ feedback in such a process which helps us to learn and grow. The juniors value (i) regular touchpoints over one-off initiatives, (ii) a genuine safe space to speak up, and (iii) transparency from seniors who are willing to “open the black box” and explain the why behind decisions. Many juniors are managing high performance expectations alongside their desired need for balance. FORUM Manoj Bhargava co-Singapore managing partner, Sidley Austin Calvin Chow partner, PC Woo & Co Gerard Quek deputy managing partner, PDLegal How is your firm using team-building initiatives as a retention tool especially with associate attrition remaining a persistent challenge? What types of programs resonate most with your lawyers? Leading law firms in Asia are keeping their best talent by ditching the old playbook and focusing on what actually matters - clear career paths, mental health support, and building real connections at work. The Briefs
6 Asian Legal Business | November 2025 The Briefs Global trade war propels Singapore’s surge as maritime arbitration hub Singapore is cementing its position as a leading maritime arbitration hub, with new data revealing a dramatic surge in cases even as geopolitical tensions reshape global shipping and trade patterns. According to a report published by law firm HFW, the Singapore Chamber of Maritime Arbitration (SCMA) recorded 95 new case references in 2024, a 73 percent year-over-year increase, and a 112 percent increase over its five-year average caseload. This growth trajectory is unfolding against a backdrop of Singapore’s steady expansion in the global maritime arbitration market. The city-state’s maritime arbitration caseload has grown from approximately five percent of London’s volume in 2022 to nine percent in 2024. Over the past 15 years, Singapore has progressively increased its share of global maritime arbitration, sometimes at the expense of traditional hubs like London and New York. “When [UK law firm] Hill Dickinson established its Singapore office in 2009, approximately 95 percent of our arbitration work related to London arbitrations; today, that figure is closer to 50 percent,” reveals Peter Doraisamy, group managing partner at PD Legal, which operates in a formal law alliance with Hill Dickinson. As Singapore’s market share expands, law firms are adapting their strategies to meet growing demand. For example, Bazul Ashhab, managing partner and head of dispute resolution at Oon & Bazul, explains that the firm’s shipping arbitration practice “was built around Singapore’s rise as a global maritime hub,” with the firm scaling its team through targeted recruitment of senior disputes lawyers and closer collaboration with technical and industry experts. The firm has also deployed a dedicated strategy analyst to track dispute triggers in shipbuilding and financing, allowing it to “anticipate developments before they reach the tribunal stage.” These preparations are particularly timely given the escalating SinoU.S. trade war, which is creating new pressures on maritime contracts. “With shifting geopolitics, sanctions are increasingly driving contract cancellations and supply-chain breakdowns,” Bazul observes. For clients navigating these tensions, dispute resolution clause design has become significantly more complex. “Enforcement exposure, sanctions, and counterparty domicile now shape clause design alongside governing law and seat,” says Bazul. He often recommends hybrid structures combining sector-specific rules with a neutral, enforceable seat such as Singapore to balance efficiency, neutrality, and enforceability. Doraisamy emphasizes that there is no one-size-fits-all solution in this environment. “Where a non-Chinese domiciled party contracts with a Chinese domiciled counterparty, a Hong Kongseated arbitration before a qualified arbitral institution such as the HKIAC is often prudent,” he explains, noting this permits interim relief from mainland Chinese courts in support of arbitration. However, he adds that hybrid arrangements are also increasingly common, such as a Hong Kong seated arbitration applying the LMAA Rules, with hearings in Singapore under English law, depending on the parties’ commercial needs. As Hong Kong and Singapore compete for trade-war-related maritime disputes - with Hong Kong ranked joint-second globally as a preferred arbitration seat alongside Singapore - the question of competitive differentiation has become increasingly important. For Bazul, Singapore’s neutrality has emerged as a key differentiator. “Singapore’s neutrality has become its defining strategic advantage,” Ashhab states. “Amid U.S.–China tensions, parties want a forum independent of major power blocs yet anchored in strong judicial infrastructure.” Doraisamy, however, views the competition between these jurisdictions through a complementary lens. What distinguishes his Singapore practice, he argues, is “not merely geography but depth of sectoral expertise.” This focus on sectoral specialization reflects a broader strategic choice in how firms position themselves in an evolving market. “We have observed a trend toward lawyers presenting themselves primarily as international arbitration specialists, rather than sector specialists,” Doraisamy notes. However, the HFW report’s observation of a shift “from dominance by a few traditional hubs to a more even global distribution” of maritime arbitration reflects a fundamental transformation in how and where disputes are resolved. “The redistribution of maritime arbitration from a few traditional hubs toward a more globalised landscape is unmistakable,” Doraisamy says, noting that while earlier Australian practitioners may have joked that “international arbitration would never take off in Australia – we all like travelling to London too much!”, the current environment proves otherwise.

8 Asian Legal Business | November 2025 THE Q&A The Briefs Sunny Mann was recently appointed as Baker McKenzie’s global chair. In this interview, he shares insights on navigating geopolitical disruption, leveraging the firm’s deep expertise in international trade and sanctions, and capitalizing on emerging opportunities in India’s rapidly liberalizing legal market. Sunny Mann, Baker McKenzie ALB: How will your background as global chair of Baker McKenzie’s International Trade Practice Group inform your approach to helping clients navigate today’s fragmented global trade landscape? Sunny Mann: We must continue to ensure that our clients are not just reactive to change and disruption but are proactively positioned to thrive amidst uncertainty. While I was global chair of Baker McKenzie’s International Trade Practice Group and chair of the firm’s Geopolitical Risks Taskforce in recent years, I had a front-row seat to the profound shifts and evolving complexities of international trade patterns, and the increasingly disruptive impact these changes are having on our clients’ business strategies. Our team operates across 40+ jurisdictions – in doing so, we have developed a deep understanding of how geopolitics, sanctions, tariffs, and trade barriers can impact cross-border business operations, including supply chains and investment decisions. We are more than just legal counsel - we are trusted partners who help clients anticipate and respond to a rapidly changing geopolitical environment, offering clients holistic guidance that integrates legal, strategic, business and operational considerations. Since inception, Baker McKenzie has nurtured a globalised appetite to take on the toughest and most complex problems our clients face. Nowhere is this more evident than with the disruption caused by AI, where that mindset aligns with our early adopter advantage (we began investing in AI seriously way back in 2017) and our incredible expertise in that field, leading to some massive wins on highly complicated matters for our clients. ALB: Based on your expertise in export controls and sanctions across multiple jurisdictions, what do you see as the most critical geopolitical tensions currently reshaping global commerce? Mann: Businesses operating across borders are having to contend with a landscape where trade rules are increasingly blurred and politicised. The multilateral institutions and frameworks that have underpinned global trade since the late 1940s are increasingly being called into doubt, while longstanding trade partnerships are being replaced by a complex patchwork of bilateral and regional agreements. In parallel, trade is becoming a tool of national security and strategic foreign policy. For example, export restrictions on critical minerals or strategic technologies - often framed as national security measures - can have ripple effects across supply chains. Baker McKenzie has the geographical footprint and depth of local market understanding to help clients make the most of the new bilateral trade and investment corridors, while navigating the nuance of the local national security landscape in each of these different countries. ALB: Baker McKenzie has one of the largest India practices among international firms. How do you plan to develop this practice further in the wake of the latest liberalisation efforts by the Bar Council of India? Mann: I am of proud Indian heritage and incredibly excited by the opportunities that India offers our clients and our firm. India is at a truly pivotal moment, projected to become the world’s third-largest economy by 2027. At the same time, the Indian legal market is on the brink of its most significant transformation in decades, following the recent liberalisation efforts by the Bar Council of India (BCI). As a firm, we are very supportive of the great work being undertaken by the BCI. Baker McKenzie already plays a pivotal role with around 300 lawyers across more than 70 offices supporting Indian and multinational clients on India-related matters. We plan to open our India office under the new BCI rules at the earliest opportunity to support our clients and further deepen our long-standing commitment to the Indian market. In the meantime, we will continue to utilise our fly-in-fly-out model to help our clients capitalise on India’s growth potential, business opportunities, and mitigate risks, as we have done for over 60 years.
9 Asian Legal Business | November 2025 The Briefs Singapore faces cross-border DeFi identity verification challenge Singapore’s ambition to become Asia’s virtual assets hub faces a new test as global regulators eye revolutionary privacy technology that could fundamentally alter how financial institutions verify customer identities in decentralised finance. Zero-knowledge proofs, advanced cryptographic protocols that allow one party to prove the validity of a statement without revealing underlying data, have caught the attention of the U.S. Treasury as a potential solution for bringing compliance to the Wild West of DeFi. While the technology promises to address anti-money laundering and sanctions compliance while maximising user privacy, it’s creating a complex puzzle for Singapore-based institutions operating across both jurisdictions. “Zero-knowledge Proofs are advanced cryptographic protocols that allow one party to prove the validity of a statement to another party without revealing any underlying data,” explain Chua Tju Liang, head and director of blockchain and digital assets, and Ulanda Oon, associate director of corporate and finance at Drew & Napier. “In digital identity applications, ZKPs enable users to demonstrate compliance with certain requirements (such as age, residency, or KYC status) without sharing their full personal information.” The U.S. Treasury, directed by the GENIUS Act to seek public comment on incorporating digital identity verification into transaction execution processes, has signalled strong interest in implementing such measures. Though no specific regulation has been proposed yet, the implications for Singapore-based firms are already becoming clear. If mandatory digital ID verification comes to fruition in the United States, Singapore-based clients serving U.S. users may find themselves caught between two regulatory worlds. The challenge stems from fundamental differences in how each jurisdiction approaches customer verification. Under Singapore’s regulatory framework, payment service providers, including digital payment service providers and decentralised exchange operators, must comply with obligations specified in MAS Notice PSN02. These requirements are decidedly traditional: collecting and verifying full names, identification numbers, residential addresses, dates of birth, and nationality for individuals, plus incorporation details and ownership structures for legal entities. “If the U.S. Treasury’s proposal to mandate digital ID verification prior to transaction execution in DeFi smart contracts comes to fruition, potentially through the use of ZKPs, at the infrastructure level, Singapore-based clients serving U.S. users may have to adopt a cumulative approach towards complying with the requirements of both jurisdictions,” say Chua and Oon. This means that even if zeroknowledge proofs can verify identity for money laundering screening and sanctions compliance, “the current obligation under the MAS Notice PSN02 still requires such payment service providers to collect underlying identification documents, resulting in a cumulative (i.e. dual) compliance requirement.” The apparent conflict between privacy-preserving technology and traditional KYC requirements may not be insurmountable. Legal experts point to a hybrid model that could satisfy both jurisdictions’ demands. In this approach, users would first complete a traditional onboarding phase, submitting personally identifiable information to a trusted ID issuer. This information, such as name, age, and sanctions status, would be encrypted and stored in a way that allows verification through zero-knowledge proofs without repeated disclosure. “Through this hybrid approach, while PII may still be collected during the Traditional Onboarding Phase to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements imposed under Singapore law, such ZKP integration can help service providers minimise the amount of PII they access or process during routine transactions,” note Chua and Oon. For financial institutions, the message is clear: Start preparing now. There’s a possibility that future regulations could create direct conflicts between jurisdictions, one prohibiting the collection and retention of underlying personal data, another requiring institutions to collect and retain such information for reporting purposes. Institutions should consider developing data collection frameworks that could apply differently to users in different markets, anticipating potential conflicts between privacy-preserving mandates and traditional disclosure requirements. Chua and Oon recommend closely monitoring developments from MAS, international standard-setters, including the Financial Action Task Force, and key foreign regulators. “We regard it as a priority for financial institutions to consider how existing obligations for AML/CFT compliance, and protection of personal data might interact with ZKP-based identity verification approaches,” they say.
10 Asian Legal Business | November 2025 The Briefs Regulatory scrutiny intensifies amid Hong Kong commercial real estate crisis The skyline hasn’t changed as Hong Kong’s office towers still pierce the clouds with their characteristic ambition. But what was once an unshakeable pillar of Asia’s financial capital now resembles a widening chasm in its core economic landscape. The numbers tell a story of accelerating distress in the city’s commercial real estate sector. Hang Seng Bank’s impaired loans exploded to 6.7 percent of gross loans by June 2025, more than doubling from 2.8 percent at the end of 2023 - a deterioration believed to have catalysed HSBC’s $13.6 billion privatisation proposal for its struggling subsidiary. This is not a crisis born from a single shock, according to Roy Leung and Simon Siu, partners at Sit, Fung, Kwong & Shum (SFKS). “Today’s situation involves a complex interplay of factors, including sustained relatively high global interest rates, a more cautious appetite towards property market, a retreat of red capital, and the impacts of Chinese mainland’s property adjustments,” they explain. The physical market fundamentals compound these financial pressures. Prime office rents have plummeted over 20 percent since 2022, with vacancy rates climbing to 19 percent as new completions flood an already oversupplied market. The crisis affects developers differently depending on their size and resources. “While SME developers are facing liquidity challenges due to more tightened bank credit, larger developers are actively engaging in strategic deleveraging, such as asset sales, to secure refinancing opportunities,” Leung and Siu note. Simon Reid-Kay, principal of Simon Reid-Kay & Associates, points out that many borrowers are locked in low-rate mortgages during the pandemic era, creating a peculiar disincentive to refinance. As a result, “refinancing activity is more selective, often driven by needs to cash-out or refinancing of recent shorter-term but higher-rate loans.” More fundamentally, “structural changes in capital market, such as tighter liquidity, reduced bank lending, and increased reliance on private credit, have raised the likelihood of developers defaulting. Limited access to refinancing and higher interest rates strain cash flows,” Reid-Kay adds. Lenders and borrowers are now increasingly engaging in workouts due to maturing commercial real estate loans and tighter capital markets. Leung and Siu observe that debt resolutions are “increasingly becoming collaborative efforts”, calling it “a paradigm shift from zero-sum creditor-debtor conflicts toward potentially positive-sum solutions.” However, Reid-Kay observes that traditional workout strategies, such as debt restructuring or asset sales, are less viable due to lower asset valuations and fewer willing buyers. “New approaches, such as equity injections or joint ventures, may be considered as alternatives,” he notes. “Admittedly, a majority of workout attempts did not materialise after exploratory stage,” says Leung and Siu. “Still, creditors are inclined to be receptive to concrete debt restructuring proposals involving repayments by haircut and/or instalments.” With Hong Kong’s commercial real estate sector navigating this complex landscape marked by ongoing adjustments in property prices, a high-rate environment, rising non-performing loans and economic uncertainties, regulatory scrutiny has intensified accordingly. “While the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is closely monitoring these developments, it has repeatedly assured that the overall credit risk landscape remains manageable, citing the strong capital and liquidity positions and resilience of Hong Kong’s banking system and the fact that most of the CRE loans are made to sizeable developers that are financially solid,” say Leung and Siu. However, coordination among regulators is tightening. The SFKS partners note that the Securities and Futures Commission, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, and the Accounting and Financial Reporting Council have strengthened collaboration in the regulation of listed issuers’ financial activities and the related work of auditors. “We do not think that Hong Kong is currently at the brink of triggering systemic crisis protocols, but regulators are on alert,” says Reid-Kay. “While interventionist measures have not been activated, the regulators continue to be cautious and proactive, especially amid global volatility and geopolitical tensions.” This development is also reshaping Hong Kong’s legal services market. “Law firms are implementing strategic adaptations to mitigate the downturn in property-related services, such as diversifying into other practice areas, allowing firms to balance their portfolios,” Leung and Siu note.

12 Asian Legal Business | November 2025 The Briefs Can the Philippines compete for Asian capital with its tax reforms? While much of the world debates how to tax capital markets more heavily, the Philippines is moving in the opposite direction. With the Capital Markets Efficiency Promotion Act taking effect on July 1, 2025, the Southeast Asian country has bet on lower taxes and simpler rules to lure both global fund managers and everyday Filipino investors into a market that has long played second fiddle to regional hubs like Singapore and Hong Kong. 1 How will the new capital gains tax change crossborder deal-making? The legislation, known as CMEPA or Republic Act No. 12214, represents a wholesale reimagining of how the Philippines taxes investment activity. One of the key amendments under the law is the uniform 15 percent capital gains tax on the sale of unlisted foreign shares, which now matches the rate for domestic unlisted shares. “This harmonization reduces the incentive for structuring deals via foreign entities to exploit lower tax rates, simplifying transaction planning and reducing regulatory arbitrage”, explain Alain Charles J. Veloso, M&A partner at Quisumbing Torres, member firm of Baker McKenzie in the Philippines, and Micah Mirra A. Borja, associate at the firm. However, Veloso and Borja note that “the increased tax burden on foreign share sales may prompt parties to reconsider transaction valuations and deal terms, requiring advisors to provide a more nuanced, jurisdiction-specific advice.” 2Will the cut in stock transaction taxes actually boost trading volumes? In addition, one of the most impactful changes is CMEPA’s significant reduction of the stock transaction tax. The STT on listed shares has been slashed from 0.6 percent to 0.1percent – that’s an 83 percent reduction that brings the Philippines more in line with regional competitors. “For foreign institutional investors, the lower STT is expected to increase the volume of securities transactions, as trading becomes more cost-effective,” Veloso and Borja observe. They anticipate this will generate increased demand for both routine and complex transaction advisory work, though it may also introduce new complexities around due diligence and regulatory disclosure requirements. Critically, “the lower STT aligns the Philippines more closely with regional peers, making it a more attractive venue for large-scale securities investment and trading,” add Veloso and Borja. Specifically, lawyers believe CMEPA positions the Philippines more competitively within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a critical consideration as the region continues to attract global capital. “The Philippines is expected to attract a greater share of cross-border portfolio flows, especially from global funds seeking exposure to emerging Southeast Asian markets,” note Veloso and Borja. 3How will local retail investors fare as foreign capital floods in? While attracting foreign capital is a priority, CMEPA also aims to ensure that international investment doesn’t come at the expense of domestic retail investors. A key objective of the legislation is ensuring that increased foreign investment complements rather than displaces local market participation, according to lawyers. “By treating foreign and domestic transactions equitably, CMEPA helps maintain a level playing field, preventing local investors from being crowded out by large foreign funds,” note Veloso and Borja. This equitable treatment also builds investor confidence, as retail participants can better anticipate returns and make informed decisions, fostering what the lawyers describe as “a more inclusive and resilient capital market ecosystem.” As a result, CMEPA’s commitment to more efficient capital markets is expected to drive robust demand for specialized legal services, with Philippine law firms playing a key role in advising both domestic and foreign clients on complex transactions, regulatory compliance, and dispute resolution. “As foreign fund managers seek to compete within ASEAN markets, they will increasingly rely on local legal expertise to navigate the evolving landscape, structure innovative investment products, and ensure adherence to best practices,” say Veloso and Borja. EXPLAINER
13 Asian Legal Business | November 2025 The Briefs A listing in Astana: Chinese companies explore diverse financing strategies Chinese companies are diversifying their overseas expansion, with financing strategies evolving to reflect this shift. On Aug. 28, tungsten miner Jiaxin International Resources Investment made history with a dual listing on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX) and the Astana International Exchange’s (AIX) Belt and Road Market in Kazakhstan. This marked the world’s first Hong KongKazakhstan listing and the first on AIX’s Belt and Road board. Founded in Hong Kong in 2014, Jiaxin focuses on the Bakuta tungsten mine in Kazakhstan. Major shareholders include state-owned giants Jiangxi Copper and China Railway Construction Corp. Kazakhstan borders China’s Xinjiang, and a railway connects Khorgos port directly to Almaty, placing the Bakuta mine just 20 kilometers from the line. Once operational, this rail access will streamline transportation. “In Jiaxin’s Hong Kong IPO, some international placement shares were listed on AIX, with trading in Hong Kong dollars on HKEX and Renminbi on AIX,” says Tim Wang, partner and Chair of China Practice of Clifford Chance, which advised Jiaxin on Hong Kong and U.S. legal matters. Traditionally, international placement shares in a Hong Kong IPO are only traded on HKEX, making the AIX listing a pioneering move. However, since the two exchanges lack mutual recognition, Jiaxin employed a parallel issuance and separate filing structure to comply with regulators in mainland China, Hong Kong, and Kazakhstan, explains Guo Shifang, partner at Global Law Office, which served as Jiaxin’s Chinese counsel. In 2018, to attract international investment, Kazakhstan established the Astana International Exchange (AIX) in addition to the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE), which had been focused on domestic investment. As of the end of 2024, although it ranks 62nd globally in terms of financing, AIX has surpassed exchanges in Prague, Warsaw, Istanbul, and Budapest, emerging as the leading financing centre in Central Asia and Eastern Europe. Jiaxin’s AIX listing signals bold new choices for Chinese companies in foreign capital markets. Wang observes that while Chinese firms continue to prioritize traditional markets like Hong Kong, they are increasingly exploring diversified, regional capital market options. “Companies consider other markets based on their business strategies, geopolitical factors, industry characteristics, and specific project needs,” he says. Jiaxin is a prime example of this approach. Additionally, companies with a focus in Europe often opt for GDR listings in markets like Switzerland and London to expand their investor base. Guo shares similar observations. “In the past, Chinese companies mainly listed in Hong Kong and the U.S., with some in Singapore, the U.K., and Canada. But in recent years, geopolitical shifts have prompted some firms to list in nontraditional markets.” And there are other reasons, such as differences in valuation models—certain markets offer higher pricing premiums for sectors like new energy, mining, and agriculture—or lower listing and compliance costs compared to U.S. or Hong Kong markets. “Political and strategic considerations also play a role,” she says, noting that companies evaluate diplomatic relations and trade agreements to assess the ease of local and cross-border activities. Law firms have also expanded services to meet these demands. Recently, there have been articles on law firm WeChat platforms about listings in Indonesia, Malaysia, Dubai, and even Latin America. While diverse listing options offer significant benefits, Jiaxin’s project involves considerable complexity. To meet multiple regulatory requirements, the company and its sponsors engage seven legal teams across China, Hong Kong, Kazakhstan, Luxembourg, and other jurisdictions, leading to higher costs. However, Guo believes that in the future, cross-border financing and capital operations in sectors like energy, resources, and infrastructure under the Belt and Road framework will grow. As Hong Kong strengthens its role as a global connector, combinations like Hong Kong + Central Asia or Hong Kong + the Middle East could create niche markets, challenging capital market lawyers to coordinate across jurisdictions and navigate emerging market legal systems. Wang agrees, predicting that dual listings, especially in emerging financing markets, will present new legal, regulatory, and technical challenges, requiring law firms and intermediaries to have strong global networks and cross-jurisdictional coordination skills. “This could become a competitive advantage for international firms, while also exploring new paths to solidify Hong Kong’s position in global capital markets,” he says.

docs.content:
(UPDATE) KUALA LUMPUR — East Timor joined the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) bloc as its 11th member state on Sunday, after 14 years of campaigning.
Its Prime Minister Xanana Gusmao joined Asean leaders for a summit and signing ceremony in the Malaysian capital, before posing for photographs together with interlocking arms.

docs.title: Timor - Leste becomes 11th member of ASEAN
docs.snippet: Kuala Lumpur, Oct 26 : Timor-Leste became the 11th member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) during the 47th ASEAN Summit in Malays...
docs.content:
Kuala Lumpur, Oct 26 : Timor-Leste became the 11th member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) during the 47th ASEAN Summit in Malaysia's Kuala Lumpur on Sunday.
Timor-Leste applied for ASEAN membership in 2011. In 2022, the group's leaders agreed in principle to include Timor-Leste as a member state, granting it Observer Status in ASEAN meetings. This was followed by the adoption of the Roadmap for Timor-Leste's Full Membership in 2023, which guided its preparations to meet ASEAN's membership criteria, including accession to ASEAN legal instruments and participation in meetings across all three ASEAN Community pillars.
In a statement, ASEAN stated, "In a historic occasion for the region, the Signing of the Declaration on the Admission of Timor-Leste into ASEAN took place at the Opening Ceremony of the 47th ASEAN Summits and Related Summits, held on 26 October 2025. The Declaration was signed by ASEAN Leaders together with the Prime Minister of Timor-Leste, marking the ASEAN Leaders' consent to accept Timor-Leste as the 11th Member State of ASEAN. This achievement is the result of years of close cooperation between ASEAN and Timor-Leste."
Timor-Leste's Prime Minister Xanana Gusmao joined the ASEAN leaders for the signing of documents confirming the nation's inclusion in the bloc. The leaders then posed for a family picture. This is the first expansion in the group since 1999.
The ASEAN was established in Thailand's Bangkok in 1967, with the signing of the ASEAN Declaration (Bangkok Declaration) by the Founding Fathers of ASEAN: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. Brunei Darussalam joined ASEAN in 1984, followed by Vietnam in 1995, Laos and Myanmar in 1997, and Cambodia in 1999.
Malaysia, as the Chair of ASEAN, is hosting the 47th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits under the theme "Inclusivity and Sustainability" in Kuala Lumpur from October 26-28.
These Summits consist of the ASEAN Summit, the ASEAN Plus One Summits between ASEAN and seven Dialogue Partners, namely, Australia, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia, the US, respectively, as well as the ASEAN Plus Three Summit, East Asia Summit, ASEAN-United Nations Summit and ASEAN-New Zealand Commemorative Summit to mark 50 years of dialogue relations, according to the official statement. Malaysia will also host the 5th Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) Summit and 3rd Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) Leaders Meeting at the sidelines of the Summits.

docs.content:
Can't find what you're looking for?
View all search resultsCan't find what you're looking for?
View all search resultsMembership of ASEAN brings Timor-Leste political visibility and economic opportunity, but also new exposure to disputes in a grouping where several members are wrestling with democratic backsliding.
imor-Leste’s admission to ASEAN ends more than 12 years of waiting and inaugurates a new phase in the country’s regional engagement. The inclusion in ASEAN of its 11th member comes at a time of heightened geopolitical and economic pressures for the regional bloc as it navigates internal tensions and uncertainty in the Indo-Pacific.
Membership offers Asia’s youngest country access to new political and economic opportunities, but also exposes it to the same regional challenges that dominate ASEAN’s agenda. These include tensions in the South China Sea, great-power rivalry, climate risks and transnational crime.
While it has championed democracy and freedom, Timor-Leste also faces structural challenges including inequality and unemployment. In the next few years, the country needs to work strategically on the following three points.
Timor-Leste is the only state in South East Asia categorized as “free” by the Freedom House Index, and has maintained a score of 72/100 on the aggregate of political rights and civil liberties since 2021. This is a stark difference to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, its much larger and older democratic neighbors who have far lower scores and are deemed only “partially free”.
A study notes that leaders such as Timor-Leste Prime Minister Xanana Gusmão and President José Ramos-Horta are known for their outspoken and independent traits that may stand out in an ASEAN setting where consensus is the main aim of discussions. Although their outspokenness could spark hopes for a more democratic region, this difference is also a reason for Timor-Leste to tread carefully while it navigates ASEANs varied political landscape.
Several of the bloc’s current members are currently facing challenges in their democratic functioning.
The 2024 presidential election in Indonesia became controversial when a Constitutional Court decision, accused of being politically motivated, altered age criteria that eventually allowed then-president Joko “Jokowi” Widodo’s son to run for vice-president.
Malaysia’s democracy faced a significant setback with the collapse of the reformist Pakatan Harapan (PH) government in February 2020, just 22 months after its historic election victory.
The Philippines is also dealing with systemic corruption and the dominance of powerful political dynasties at national and local levels that undermine true democratic competition and accountability.
ASEAN member states have divergent positions toward responses to regional developments and crisis situations. Their diverse foreign policies place ASEAN states into three main categories: those who are “concerned”; those who prefer maintaining “neutrality”; and the “clearly aligned”. This makes a unified position very unlikely in times of tensions.
Against this backdrop, Timor-Leste must quickly strategize how it wishes to navigate its complex environment. On the one hand, it must show solidarity with its neighbors. On the other, China’s much stronger presence in Timor-Leste may compel it to think of optimal hedging strategies.
Timor-Leste’s concern in the Indo-Pacific is not as pronounced as its neighbors. While larger countries like Indonesia and the Philippines view the Indo-Pacific as a theater of political-security prowess among nations, Timor-Leste is mainly focused on the development aspect of this “imaginary political region” and the potential economic advantages that it brings for it as an individual actor.
It does not yet have a strong enough military presence for it to be considered as a threat and is therefore mostly viewed as a “partner” to great powers in the region. While this situation may not be worrying today, a lack of solidarity with ASEAN will increasingly make Timor-Leste a potential ally to any competing great power and sharpen the divide among ASEAN member states.
In an interview, President Ramos-Horta expressed Timor-Leste’s commitment to hosting its first ASEAN Summit by 2029. This commitment will be one that will either make or break Timor-Leste as it navigates the region’s most critical issues while maintaining capable leadership.
The summit is an expensive event to hold with year-round activities, carefully thought-through logistics for events taking place across the country, and security. Indonesia is reported to have budgeted Rp 95.24 billion (US$6.1 million) for the summits it held in 2023. Malaysia budgeted 12 million ringgit ($2.1 million) for the 46th ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly General Assembly this year.
The Philippines is preparing a whopping 17.495 billion peso ($302 million) budget for the summits and related meetings to be held in 2026. These numbers are a telling sign of how much ASEAN states are prepared to invest in leading delicate decision-making processes in the region while projecting national capabilities.
Beyond concerns of budget, Timor-Leste will need to quickly increase its staffing numbers ahead of 2029 across all sectors particularly in the ASEAN Political-Security Community (APSC) and ASEAN Economic Community (AEC). To ensure a successful chairmanship, it will rely heavily on its ability to engage in discussions meaningfully through capacity and bureaucratic efficiency.
Chairmanship is not only about hosting discussions. It is fundamentally about implementing regional commitments.
While Timor-Leste can take pride in the success of one of its big foreign policy goals, these critical priorities need early strategizing. The time for Timor-Leste to prepare is now, and more critically in 2028 when it becomes a part of the ASEAN Troika with the incumbent and former chairs of ASEAN.
---
The writer is the managing director of the ASEAN Studies Centre and a lecturer in international relations at Gadjah Mada University. The article is republished under a Creative Commons license.

docs.title: Timor - Leste becomes 11th member of ASEAN
docs.snippet: Kuala Lumpur, Oct 26 : Timor-Leste became the 11th member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) during the 47th ASEAN Summit in Malays...
docs.content:
Kuala Lumpur, Oct 26 : Timor-Leste became the 11th member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) during the 47th ASEAN Summit in Malaysia's Kuala Lumpur on Sunday.
Timor-Leste applied for ASEAN membership in 2011. In 2022, the group's leaders agreed in principle to include Timor-Leste as a member state, granting it Observer Status in ASEAN meetings. This was followed by the adoption of the Roadmap for Timor-Leste's Full Membership in 2023, which guided its preparations to meet ASEAN's membership criteria, including accession to ASEAN legal instruments and participation in meetings across all three ASEAN Community pillars.
In a statement, ASEAN stated, "In a historic occasion for the region, the Signing of the Declaration on the Admission of Timor-Leste into ASEAN took place at the Opening Ceremony of the 47th ASEAN Summits and Related Summits, held on 26 October 2025. The Declaration was signed by ASEAN Leaders together with the Prime Minister of Timor-Leste, marking the ASEAN Leaders' consent to accept Timor-Leste as the 11th Member State of ASEAN. This achievement is the result of years of close cooperation between ASEAN and Timor-Leste."
Timor-Leste's Prime Minister Xanana Gusmao joined the ASEAN leaders for the signing of documents confirming the nation's inclusion in the bloc. The leaders then posed for a family picture. This is the first expansion in the group since 1999.
The ASEAN was established in Thailand's Bangkok in 1967, with the signing of the ASEAN Declaration (Bangkok Declaration) by the Founding Fathers of ASEAN: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. Brunei Darussalam joined ASEAN in 1984, followed by Vietnam in 1995, Laos and Myanmar in 1997, and Cambodia in 1999.
Malaysia, as the Chair of ASEAN, is hosting the 47th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits under the theme "Inclusivity and Sustainability" in Kuala Lumpur from October 26-28.
These Summits consist of the ASEAN Summit, the ASEAN Plus One Summits between ASEAN and seven Dialogue Partners, namely, Australia, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia, the US, respectively, as well as the ASEAN Plus Three Summit, East Asia Summit, ASEAN-United Nations Summit and ASEAN-New Zealand Commemorative Summit to mark 50 years of dialogue relations, according to the official statement. Malaysia will also host the 5th Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) Summit and 3rd Asia Zero Emission Community (AZEC) Leaders Meeting at the sidelines of the Summits.

docs.content:
Cambodia Committed for a Resilient and Inclusive ASEAN Community
AKP Phnom Penh, October 27, 2025 --
At the 47th ASEAN Summit held in Kuala Lumpur on Oct. 26, Prime Minister Samdech Moha Borvor Thipadei Hun Manet reaffirmed Cambodia’s commitment to contributing to ASEAN’s community-building efforts toward the realisation of a resilient, innovative, inclusive, and people-centred Community, in line with the ASEAN Community Vision 2045: Our Shared Future.
According to a press release from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, in his address, Samdech Thipadei, commended Malaysia for its exemplary Chairmanship of ASEAN this year. He highlighted that under Malaysia’s leadership, the region has continued to move forward with unity, resilience, and purpose. He expressed Cambodia’s deep appreciation to Prime Minister H.E. Dato’ Seri Anwar Ibrahim for his personal leadership and steadfast commitment in facilitating the peaceful resolution of the Cambodia-Thailand dispute.
Samdech Thipadei further lauded Malaysia’s resolute dedication to regional peace and stability, reflected through its constructive facilitation and hosting of the four-party talks on the Peace Deal proposed by President Donald Trump, which was officially signed in Kuala Lumpur — a development marking a new milestone in ASEAN’s diplomatic achievements.
Samdech Thipadei warmly welcomed the historic admission of Timor-Leste as ASEAN’s 11th member, describing it as a testament to ASEAN’s enduring strength and inclusiveness. He noted that this achievement signifies the organisation’s determination to deepen regional integration, injecting renewed energy and dynamism into the ASEAN Community-building process.
Amid global uncertainties, Samdech Thipadei further underscored that, despite resurgent global conflicts, ASEAN continues to stand as a region of peace and stability that upholds dialogue over confrontation, peaceful means over coercion, and international law over unilateral action renouncing the threat or use of force and uphold the core principles of the UN Charter and the ASEAN Charter.
By Heng Panha

docs.title: 2025 – successful year for ASEAN : Deputy FM
docs.snippet: Hanoi (VNA) – The year 2025 marks a successful period for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), with a series of historic milestones ach...
docs.content:
Hanoi (VNA) – The year 2025 marks a successful period for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), with a series of historic milestones achieved, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Dang Hoang Giang has said.
Giang, who is also head of Vietnam’s SOM ASEAN, made the remarks at an inter-sectoral meeting in Hanoi on December 9 to review cooperation, Vietnam’s participation in 2025, and orientations for 2026. Nearly 60 delegates from ministries and sectors took part.
According to the official, ASEAN has laid out a strategic cooperation framework for the next two decades on the basis of major achievements and strong progress in Community-building. These include the adoption of the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 and strategies across political-security, economic, socio-cultural and connectivity pillars, all aimed at building a resilient, innovative, dynamic and people-centred ASEAN.
He stressed that the admission of Timor-Leste as ASEAN’s 11th member marked the bloc’s first expansion in almost 30 years, widening its geographical reach and strengthening its collective capacity.
Economic, trade and investment linkages continued to be enhanced through the upgrading of the ASEAN Trade in Goods Agreement, the development of the ASEAN Sustainable Investment Guidelines and the basic completion of negotiations on the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement.
ASEAN’s cooperation with its development partners remained strong and substantive in 2025. Highlights included the establishment of a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with New Zealand; the upgrading of free trade agreements with China, the Republic of Korea and India; the implementation of upgraded FTAs with Australia and New Zealand; and the acceleration of negotiations on an FTA with Canada, scheduled for completion in 2026. ASEAN’s role as a symbol of dialogue and cooperation for peace, security and development continues to be widely recognised, he said.
For Vietnam, Giang noted, 2025 provided an opportunity to look back on three decades of its engagement with ASEAN. From the humble beginnings, Vietnam has become an indispensable member making significant contributions to the bloc’s shared success.
During the year, Vietnam’s senior leaders took part in numerous ASEAN activities, demonstrating the country’s strong political commitment to regional cooperation. Vietnam worked closely with other members to complete the implementation of the ASEAN Community Blueprints 2025 and adopt the ASEAN Community Vision 2045.
The country also undertook key responsibilities such as chairing the Initiative for ASEAN Integration Task Force, hosting the Working Group on the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Strategy, and advancing various initiatives, including an ASEAN Leaders’ Declaration on strengthening the arrest of wanted criminals and seven resolutions adopted by the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly.
The ASEAN Future Forum was successfully organised for the second consecutive year, gradually becoming a “brand”, creating a space for multi-dimensional and open exchanges on essential issues concerning the future of ASEAN and the region.
Looking ahead to 2026, ministries and sectors agreed to continue promoting Vietnam’s proactive, active and responsible role in ASEAN; contributing to maintaining solidarity and unity; and helping to strengthen a favourable strategic environment for development.
Delegates highlighted the importance of addressing regional hotspots; implementing the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 and sectoral strategies; strengthening the legal framework for ASEAN cooperation; and deepening regional economic integration in key strategic areas such as infrastructure, supply chains, energy connectivity, science and technology, innovation, digital transformation and the green economy.
They emphasised the need to strengthen ASEAN’s institutional capacity and enhance coordination between AIPA channel and the government in advancing regional cooperation initiatives.
They also agreed to continue implementing the Politburo’s Conclusion No. 59-KL/TW on orientations for Vietnam’s participation in ASEAN cooperation through 2030 and work to ensure the successful organisation of the ASEAN Future Forum 2026, reaffirming its contribution to the region’s future./.

docs.title: Laos highlights strong ties with Brunei at reception
docs.snippet: BANDAR SERI BEGAWAN: The Embassy of the Lao People’s Democratic Republic in Bandar Seri Begawan hosted a reception on Monday (Dec 8) to commemorate th...
docs.content:
BANDAR SERI BEGAWAN: The Embassy of the Lao People’s Democratic Republic in Bandar Seri Begawan hosted a reception on Monday (Dec 8) to commemorate the 50th Anniversary of the Establishment of the Lao PDR, held at the Rizqun International Hotel in Gadong.
Representing Brunei as the guest of honour was Minister of Education Datin Seri Setia Dr Hajah Romaizah Md Salleh and spouse.
In his welcoming remarks, Ambassador of the Lao PDR to Brunei Darussalam Heuankeo Sangsomsak highlighted the country’s progress since its declaration of independence in 1975, noting its steady expansion of diplomatic ties and growing international profile.
He said Laos and Brunei Darussalam have enjoyed warm relations since the establishment of diplomatic ties in 1993, strengthened by regular exchanges of high-level visits.
These include the state visit of President Thongloun Sisoulith, the Brunei Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah's state visit to Laos in 2023, and visits held in conjunction with the 44th and 45th Asean Summits in Vientiane.
The ambassador also recalled the official visit of Lao Minister of Foreign Affairs Thongsavanh Phomvihane last October.
“With this positive momentum, I am confident that cooperation between Lao PDR and Brunei Darussalam will continue to flourish,” he said.
He added that the ties are further reinforced by the Sultan's invitation to Lao Prime Minister Sonexay Siphandone to undertake an official visit to Brunei, extended during their bilateral meeting at the 47th Asean Summit in Kuala Lumpur last October.
Both sides, he said, will work closely to ensure the visit next year is a success.
The ambassador noted that cooperation spans several key sectors, including diplomacy, the economy, education, defence and tourism. In line with Visit Lao Year 2026, he also invited Bruneians to explore Laos’ diverse cultural and natural attractions.
On the regional front, he reiterated that Asean remains central to Laos’ foreign policy. As Asean chair last year, Laos was committed to fostering an inclusive and sustainable future for the region.
“We deeply value the strong support from Brunei Darussalam, fellow Asean member states and our dialogue partners during Laos’ Asean chairmanship, as we work together to uphold Asean centrality and unity,” he said.
The ambassador underscored the importance of a future-oriented partnership built on trust and shared aspirations.
“Lao PDR is fully committed to strengthening relations with Brunei Darussalam for the mutual benefit of our peoples and nations,” he said, expressing confidence that longstanding ties will continue to guide both nations toward “greater peace, prosperity and harmony”.
The reception concluded with a cake-cutting ceremony by the ambassador, guest of honour and their spouses, followed by group photographs with members of the diplomatic corps. - Borneo Bulletin/ANN

topic: Nepal appoints Prime Minister via Discord poll

docs.title: A Discord - Led Democracy - Brown Political Review
docs.snippet: On September 4, the Nepali government banned dozens of social media platforms to curb dissent. Instead, the move unleashed mass nationwide protests. W...
docs.content:
On September 4, the Nepali government banned dozens of social media platforms to curb dissent. Instead, the move unleashed mass nationwide protests. Within one week, Nepal had no government—just a burnt shell of its parliament building.
Nepal’s near-total governmental collapse was primarily led by Gen Z protestors who were frustrated with systemic corruption and economic inequality under former Prime Minister Khadga Prasad Sharma Oli. In Nepal, the wealthiest 10 percent of the population has over 26 times the wealth of the poorest 40 percent and holds significant influence over the country’s politics. While Nepal’s Gen Z citizens struggle with a youth unemployment rate of over 20 percent, the children of Nepal’s politicians flaunt their wealth on social media, epitomizing the out-of-touch Oli administration. Days of mass protests led to Oli’s forced resignation, leaving a political power vacuum.
While Oli’s resignation is not unique—the country has had 14 governments in the last 17 years—Nepal’s method of forming a new government is one never seen before: a government chosen via Discord. The “Youth Against Corruption” Discord server, run by the leading protest group Hami Nepal, elected former Supreme Court judge Sushila Karki as Nepal’s next prime minister. On September 12, Karki was officially sworn in by Nepal’s president and Army Chief after meetings with Gen Z leaders. Karki is now Nepal’s first-ever female prime minister and will serve until March 2026. However, her tense relationship with Hami Nepal warns of another potential government deterioration.
Championing transparency and anti-corruption, the nonprofit organization Hami Nepal called for overthrowing the government, hoping that a democratic future might be possible. Founded in response to a devastating 7.6-magnitude earthquake in 2015, Hami Nepal acted as a crisis network, delivering direct assistance from donors to Nepalis in need. Yet, during Nepal’s protests, Hami Nepal shifted from providing aid to centralizing information and mobilizing protestors. Hami Nepal was a leading force in mobilizing Nepal’s protests alongside other groups, using its Discord server with over 150,000 members as a key organizing platform. Due to its anonymity, protestors viewed Discord as an ideal place to voice opinions without fear of intimidation, especially given mass police crackdowns at physical protests.
While online organizing offers many benefits, by harnessing Nepali disillusionment and centralizing information, Hami Nepal also threatens the concept of democracy in Nepal. The organization now occupies the role of “fact-maker” (and fact-dismisser) and is making strides toward political influence, suggesting that Hami Nepal seeks to become a dominant political party rather than a neutral caretaking administrator between regimes.
Hami Nepal’s motto of “For the People, By the People” reflects their push for political transparency. In real time, Hami Nepal volunteers asked its Discord users who should be considered for prime minister and contacted several influential political figures upon recommendation. Later, a series of polls established a list of candidates including Sushila Karki; Kathmandu’s popular rapper-turned-mayor, Balendrah Shah (or “Balen”); and popular cricketer Sagar Dhakal. Karki, whose fight against corruption in the police force resulted in her near-impeachment from the Supreme Court in 2017, is a symbol of longstanding integrity to voters worried about a continuously tumultuous political landscape. When a poll asked the Discord channel if they would like to create a formal petition for Karki to become prime minister, 89 percent of the nearly 7,000 voters chose ‘yes.’ Gen Z livestreamers debated the election behind Zoom icons of devils and anime-like characters, and the nominations and election for Nepal’s interim prime minister were punctuated by pregnant male emojis and GIFs of streamer IShowSpeed. The lack of seriousness among poll reactions dismisses the significance of the server: Hami Nepal successfully led an unprecedented online open election process. Gen Z Nepalis were able to debate the future of their country’s politics together and determine the direction of the country.
Nonetheless, Hami Nepal’s self-assertion as the “transparent” source of information on its Discord server and targeting of those who defy it offers one warning of the organization’s potential political dominance. The only users who can post on the server’s main channels are Hami Nepal’s moderators. Thus, it is Hami Nepal’s moderators themselves who determine what is or is not “misinformation.” As their #fact-check channel posts suggest, Hami Nepal often defends the words of their own leadership. The equality of the “democratic” server’s structure is compromised by the inability of non-Hami Nepal users to help dictate fact from fiction. Users could vote and debate candidates together on the server, but they could not openly rebuke Hami Nepal’s claims. Thus, by leveraging its control over communication and factual legitimacy, the organization risks creating a dangerous echo chamber where dissent is silenced.
By conflating the organization’s mission with Gen Z’s desire for democracy as a whole, Hami Nepal has the ability to target opposition groups and cement its own power within Nepali politics. A September 20 post opposing politician Mahesh Basnet accuses him of “[betraying] the sacrifices of the people and the martyrs,” invoking their image to cause agitation against sitting politicians. While Hami Nepal urges protestors not to engage in violence, they also push channel members to keep the “revolution” alive with inflammatory rhetoric. Since Karki has declared that her tenure as prime minister will end with the general elections for prime minister on March 5, 2026, Nepal’s power vacuum remains. By inflaming protestors and maintaining agitation towards politicians, Hami Nepal can manipulate this power vacuum towards their own political advantage. For example, Hami Nepal’s own Sudan Gurung announced his campaign for prime minister in the March election. Gurung even said he would topple Karki’s government, arguing that it should be transitional rather than a long-term government. While an unnamed Hami Nepal official opposed this claim, the organization’s political sway over protesters questions their stance as a broker rather than a political player.
The effects of Hami Nepal’s Discord election have manifested in political change for Nepal. In the first weeks, Karki’s government dissolved parliament and pledged to lower the voting age in March’s elections to 16. Karki’s government, while not led by Gen Z officials themselves, is guided by younger Nepalis’ desire for transparency, democracy, and equality in the country. However, even Karki may fall at the hands of Hami Nepal, the same organization that endorsed her revolutionary rise to power. Gurung, who even touched Karki’s feet to show reverence, organized Hami Nepal protests calling for her resignation just three days after she was sworn in. The fragility of Nepal’s current peace reflects the fragility of the relationship between Karki and Gurung: both have declared themselves leaders of the “people” to legitimize their political aims. Hami Nepal’s growing power and organization against Karki signals a future power grab for Gurung and continued turbulence for Nepali politics.

docs.title: The Government Was Corrupt and Willing to Kill Its Own People to Stay in Power
docs.snippet: Friday, December 19, 2025 CIVICUS discusses recent protests that led to a change of government in Nepal with Dikpal Khatri Chhetri, co-founder of Yout...
docs.content:
Friday, December 19, 2025
CIVICUS discusses recent protests that led to a change of government in Nepal with Dikpal Khatri Chhetri, co-founder of Youth in Federal Discourse (YFD). YFD is a youth-led organisation that advocates for democracy, civic engagement and young people’s empowerment.
What triggered the protests?
When the government asked social media companies to register and they failed to comply, it blocked 26 platforms, including Discord, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Signal, WhatsApp, X/Twitter and YouTube. A similar situation happened in 2023, when TikTok was banned and later reinstated once the company registered.
The government said the goal was to create a legal point of contact for content moderation and ensure platforms complied with national regulations. For them, the ban was just a matter of enforcing rules. But people saw it differently, and for Gen Z this was an attempt to silence them. Young people don’t just use social media for entertainment; it’s also where they discuss politics, expose corruption and organise themselves. By banning these platforms, the government was cutting them off from one of the few spaces where they felt they could hold leaders accountable.
However, the ban was the final factor after years of frustration with corruption, lack of accountability and a political elite that seems out of touch with ordinary people. Young people see politicians’ children living in luxury while they struggle to get by. On TikTok, this anger became visible in the ‘NepoKids’ trend that exposed the privileges of political families and tied them directly to corruption.
That’s why the response was so strong and immediate. What began as anger over a restriction on freedom of expression grew into a nationwide call for transparency, accountability and an end to the culture of corruption. Protests became a way for young people who refuse to accept the status quo to show their voices can’t be silenced.
How did the government react to the protests?
Instead of dialogue, the government chose repression. Police used rubber bullets, teargas and water cannon to try to disperse crowds. In many places they also fired live ammunition. By the end of the first day, 19 people had been killed.
The use of live ammunition against unarmed protesters is a serious violation of human rights. Authorities claimed protesters had entered restricted zones around key government buildings, including Parliament House, and argued this justified their response. But evidence tells a different story: footage and post-mortem reports show many of the victims were shot in the head, indicating an intent to inflict severe harm rather than simply disperse crowds. Police also failed to fully use non-lethal methods before turning to live bullets.
Rather than containing the protests, this violence further fuelled public anger. Protests, now focused on corruption and the killings, continued even after the government lifted the social media ban. Many realised the government was both corrupt and willing to kill its own people to stay in power. In response, authorities imposed strict curfews in big cities.
The political fallout was immediate. Home Minister Ramesh Lekhak resigned the next day, taking responsibility for the bloodshed. Within a day, Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli also stepped down. An interim government led by former Chief Justice Sushila Karki took over, parliament was dissolved and a new election is scheduled to take place in the next six months.
What changes do protesters demand and what comes next?
We are demanding systemic change. Corruption has spread through every level of government and we are tired of politicians who have ruled for decades without improving our lives. While they grow richer, everyday people face unemployment, rising living costs and no real opportunities. We refuse to accept this any longer.
We want a government that works transparently and efficiently, free from bribery, favouritism and political interference. Leaders must understand that sovereignty belongs to the people and their duty is to serve citizens, not themselves.
We need more than just some small reforms. Nepal needs serious discussions about holding to the essence of its constitution, finding ways to amend it when dissatisfaction occurs instead of uprooting it entirely. Its implementation has to be strengthened to truly include diverse voices, reflect our history and be able to respond to future challenges. We are calling for new, younger and more competent leaders who can break the cycle of past failures.
The upcoming election will be a crucial test. Gen Z must turn out in numbers, articulate clear demands to the wider public and ensure the changes we strive for in the streets are carried into parliament.

docs.content:
India Shuts Down Two Visa Application Centres In Bangladesh Over 'Security Situation'
The development comes after India summoned Bangladesh’s High Commissioner in New Delhi to issue a diplomatic protest over recent threats to the Indian High Commission in Dhaka
India on Thursday shut down two Visa Application Centers in Bangladesh’s Rajshahi and Khulna in view of the security situation in the country.
An official notification on the IVAC website read: “In view of the on-going security situation, we wish to bring to your kind notice that IVAC Rajshahi and Khulna will be closed today (18.12.2025). All applicants who have appointment slots booked for submission today will be given a slot at a later date."
Recommended Stories
The development comes after India summoned Bangladesh’s High Commissioner in New Delhi, Muhammad Riaz Hamidullah, to issue a formal diplomatic protest over recent threats to the Indian High Commission in Dhaka and inflammatory anti-India statements by Bangladeshi political leaders. In the latest instance, a leader of Bangladesh’s National Citizen Party (NCP) had threatened that Dhaka would “sever the seven sisters"—a term used to describe the country’s northeastern states—from India.
“India has close and friendly relations with the people of Bangladesh rooted in the liberation struggle and strengthened through various developmental and people-to-people initiatives. We are in favour of peace and stability in Bangladesh and have consistently called for free, fair, inclusive and credible elections, conducted in a peaceful atmosphere. We expect the interim government to ensure the safety of missions and posts in Bangladesh in keeping with its diplomatic obligations," the foreign ministry said in a statement.
The ministry earlier said India expects the interim government in Bangladesh to ensure the safety of its missions and posts in that country in keeping with its diplomatic obligations. It also noted that New Delhi is in favour of peace and stability in Bangladesh.
Three days ago, the Bangladesh foreign ministry had summoned Indian envoy to Dhaka, Pranay Verma, and conveyed its concern over former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s “incendiary" statements from Indian soil.
In its reaction, New Delhi asserted that it has never allowed its territory to be used for activities inimical to the interests of Bangladesh.
Last month, Hasina, 78, was sentenced to death by a special tribunal in Dhaka for “crimes against humanity" over her government’s crackdown on the student-led protests last year.
The Awami League leader has been living in India since she fled Bangladesh on August 5 last year in the face of the protests.
The relations between India and Bangladesh have come under strain after the interim government headed by Muhammad Yunus came to power. India has been expressing concerns over attacks on minorities, especially Hindus, in that country.
